The traffic signs are designed and positioned as supplementary means and tools for planning and determining traffic arrangements in road systems. In theory, traffic arrangements in a perfect road network could function well even without traffic signs, relying instead on conventional means of goodwill, politeness, or mutual yielding of the right of way, while adopting the behavioral rules established in T.A. 64. In practice, there exists a given road network (with its limitations) intended to serve a broad and diverse population of drivers, who, in situations of congestion, pressure, and other constraints, may lose the aforementioned conventional means, leading to "misunderstandings" or "different interpretations," which can cause disruptions, accidents, reduced capacity, and more. To ensure that everything operates smoothly, clear, simple, uniform, and unequivocal "communication" or "sign language" or "rules and regulations" are required—dictated and mandated by law—through which arrangements and rules for smooth and safe traffic will be established.

D. In general, it is preferable to place traffic signs using the "do" method. In this method, traffic arrangements are determined by the signs, which "instruct" or "guide" or "direct" or "indicate" in a "positive" message the actions that the driver can and is allowed to perform. This simplifies decision-making and facilitates the continuation of driving.  
In contrast, placement using the "do not" method through signs that prohibit with a "negative" message certain movements and actions imposes on the driver the obligation to examine the prohibitions and find the movements that remain permitted and which of them are also suitable for him. Under driving conditions with pressure from other drivers, various errors and risks may develop.

The main characteristics of the signs on the board are:  
2.1: Division into sections  
The board is composed of 10 sections, based on topic division.  
In each of them, the signs related to the topic of that section are gathered.  
Section 1 – Warning and Alert – includes the signs on this topic,  
whose purpose is to provide the driver with relevant information about the situation ahead.  
The idea is that the information will be presented "in time," so that the driver has the  
technical-physiological ability to perceive, understand, and respond correctly and in a timely manner.  
Section 2 – Instructions – includes the signs where the message is in a  
mandatory format (in command), without leaving the driver discretion and/or choice regarding the  
manner of response. This arises from the particularly severe consequences that may  
result from non-compliance with the instruction on the sign. For example: driving in the wrong direction...  
Section 3 – Right of Way – where the signs concerning the granting  
of right of way in various places and situations are gathered.  
Section 4 – Prohibitions and Restrictions – includes the signs that contain  
"prohibition" or "do not do." For example: entry prohibitions, overtaking prohibitions,  
turning or driving above the permitted speed.  
Section 5 – Public Transport – includes the signs and markings  
related to public transport and priority arrangements.

2.3: Validity  
(a) The validity of mandatory traffic signs can take four different forms.  
(1) Until the next intersection  
(2) Until canceled by another sign along the segment  
(3) Until the end of the marking that accompanies it  
(4) Until canceled by another sign in a different location, not necessarily in the same segment (also known as a "zone" sign).  
(b) The impact of jurisdictional boundaries between traffic authorities on the validity of the sign.  
(1) A jurisdictional boundary between traffic authorities exists in various combinations between adjacent local authorities, as well as between local authorities and other entities, government companies, licensees, and corporations that are local traffic authorities.  
(2) Signs placed according to Regulation 17 of the Traffic Regulations do not require the consent of the local traffic authority or prior consultation with a police officer, and therefore they are valid at their placement location on both sides of the jurisdictional boundary – regardless of it.  
(3) Signs placed according to Regulation 18 of the Traffic Regulations are based on the decision of the local traffic authority (after the consultations detailed in the regulation) and are valid only within the jurisdiction of the relevant local traffic authority. If there is an intention for the sign's instruction to apply further, beyond the jurisdictional boundary – coordination between authorities is required.

The local traffic signs (after the consultations detailed in the regulation) are valid only within the jurisdiction of the relevant local traffic authority. If there is an intention for the traffic sign to apply further, beyond the jurisdictional boundary, coordination must be made between the local traffic authorities where the sign is intended to apply continuously, on both sides of the jurisdictional boundary, while adhering to the necessary decisions and consultations accordingly. Examples: 425-424 for defining a built-up area, 427-426 for setting a special speed limit, 436-432 for defining parking prohibitions, 402, 618 for defining a one-way section. (4) When a local traffic authority is appointed to manage traffic in place, it must consult with it in decision-making, as detailed in Regulation 18. At the same time, the local traffic authority for traffic management must consult with the existing traffic authority in the area regarding traffic management arrangements it intends to establish in the area. Traffic arrangements are determined with a clear intention to ease the burden on drivers, in addition to other trends such as safety, capacity, traffic flow, etc. Uniform and simple arrangements allow for a quick understanding of the permitted and prohibited traffic directions, as well as the ability to decide and execute them well. Therefore, "correct" traffic arrangements are evaluated – among other things – by the degree of their assimilation among drivers with a minimal number of errors. Basic conditions for this are, of course, uniformity and simplicity, which combine the familiar and known with the accessible and understandable.

Section 9: Right of Way  
(64)(a) If there is no sign indicating the right of way at an intersection or a stop before approaching the intersection in the direction of travel of the vehicle, the following rules shall apply:  
(1) If several vehicles approach the intersection from different directions, the driver of a vehicle shall give the right of way to vehicles coming from the right.  
(2) A driver approaching an intersection or located at an intersection and about to turn left or make a U-turn to the left shall give the right of way to vehicles coming straight ahead and located at or near the intersection, without detracting from what is stated in paragraph (1).  
(3) A driver exiting from a dirt road and about to enter or cross a paved road shall give the right of way to vehicles approaching on the paved road.  
(b) A driver exiting from premises, from a driveway to a house, from a gas station, from a service station, from a parking place for vehicles, and the like, or from any place that is not a road, and is about to enter or cross a road -  
(1) shall slow down and, if necessary, stop to allow pedestrians to cross safely before entering the sidewalk or the shoulder of the road.  
(2) shall slow down and give the right of way to vehicles approaching on that road before entering the road.  
(c)

(1) He shall slow down and, if necessary, stop to allow pedestrians to cross safely before he gets onto the sidewalk or the shoulder of the road.  
(2) He shall slow down and give priority to vehicles approaching on the same road before entering the road.  
(c) A driver approaching an intersection or a merging of roads where a sign indicating priority for traffic on the crossing road is posted shall slow down and, if necessary, stop his vehicle to give priority to another vehicle approaching or entering the intersection or merging from another road.  
(d) A driver approaching an intersection where a stop sign is posted shall stop at a place where he can see the traffic on the crossing road, and if a stop line is marked - before the stop line, and shall give priority to another vehicle approaching or entering the intersection from another road.  
(e) A driver approaching an intersection where traffic is regulated by a traffic light shall obey the signals of the traffic light and shall not enter the intersection until a green light appears. If the traffic light shows a flashing yellow light - the driver shall slow down and, if necessary, even stop his vehicle to allow a pedestrian to complete crossing safely and shall give priority to another vehicle entering the intersection from another road, or to a vehicle approaching the intersection.

1. Meaning of the traffic signs  
Regulate the way of granting right of way to traffic in both directions, on a narrow road.  
On one side (sign 307) gives the instruction that the approaching driver must yield the right of way to the driver coming from the opposite direction. On the other side (sign 308) informs the approaching driver that he has the right of way regarding traffic from the opposite direction.  
2. Justifications for placement  
On a two-way road, in a section too narrow to serve continuous two-way traffic, and where it is not possible to regulate one-way traffic, for example:  
a. Narrow bridge  
b. A section of road where part of its width is blocked for some reason, for example: roadworks.

3. Guidelines for Placement  
A. The placement of these traffic signs must be "together" in pairs. That is, the placement of sign 308 on one side must be parallel to the placement of sign 307 at the other end of the narrow section, in order to provide the same information to drivers approaching from both directions and to prevent situations of confusion and misunderstanding between drivers traveling in opposite directions. (See in the general section, "Traffic Notice (Determination of Traffic Signs), 5771-2010", (Section 4).)  
B. In general, it is advisable to establish the right of way using these signs in a narrow and also sloped section in favor of the ascending traffic, in order to prevent a contradiction between the instructions of these signs and the instruction of Regulation 46, which grants – in the case of a sloped road – the right of way to the ascending vehicle.

171  
As mentioned, the establishment of the right of way on the ascending traffic side corresponds to the provision of Regulation 46, and therefore is seemingly unnecessary. Nevertheless, the sign should be placed in such a situation, as misunderstandings may arise between drivers in both directions due to the special conditions in the area, for example: lack of sufficient visibility.  
C. These signs will be placed near the beginning of the narrow section for which the right of way rules established by them are intended.  
They can also be placed on fixed objects at the beginning of the narrow section, such as: a guardrail, bridge, pole, tree, etc., in addition to signs 112 - 109.  
D. Sign 307 should be placed and the recommended waiting place for the vehicle should be marked – as much as possible – (by marking 810) at the closest location to the narrow section, where the road width is still sufficient to wait there, so that traffic in the opposite direction is not blocked.  
E. Signs 632 - 629 can also be added, providing information about the specific problem in the area, distances, and turns, or sign 439 with special instructions accordingly.  
F. The signs will be placed on the right side of the road, or on both sides.
The signs will be placed on the right side of the road, or on both sides.

1. Meaning of the traffic signs  
They indicate the beginning and end of a road where the right of way is granted to the vehicles traveling on it. This notification/declaration regarding the granting of the right of way on the road – explicitly and through special signage – gives the vehicles on it the legal option to take the right of way while disregarding the rules for granting the right of way detailed in Regulation 64. As is known, Regulation 64 establishes rules whose common denominator is granting the right of way and not taking it.  
2. Justifications for placement  
As a result of the contradiction between the provisions of these traffic signs and the provisions of Regulation 64, they are not placed in Israel. The mere presence of them in the "traffic sign board" stems – therefore – from the need to maintain consistency between the Israeli traffic sign board and the European traffic sign board according to the "Vienna Convention." In any case, the decision to place these traffic signs on the roads of Israel will likely involve a fundamental and special discussion. (Also, see M.M. 34).

(2) Local train (urban).  
    An electrically powered rail vehicle that runs on a pair of tracks in urban areas, sometimes in a tunnel underground and sometimes at ground level, sometimes with an exclusive right of way and sometimes alongside other road users, namely: motor vehicles, bicycles, and pedestrians.  
(3) Light rail, LRT.  
    Generally, a local train at street level, passing through the urban fabric and integrating into it.

(5) Public Transport Street (רת"צ), which allocates the entire street for the exclusive use of various public transport means. 
(6) Public Transport Route (מת"צ) - a complete lane within the street cross-section designated for public transport, exclusively for the use of buses and/or local trains on regular service lines and other passenger transport.

The sign permits heavy vehicles to cross the intersection also in other lanes specified in the sign (see column 1 of the signboard).  
Below are 3 situations in which the sign can be placed:  
Situation A - Two adjacent intersections, where the left turn is made at the second intersection. A heavy vehicle wishing to turn left can cross the first intersection in the left lane in order to make the left turn from the designated lane at the second intersection. Without sign 613, it must cross the first intersection in the rightmost lane and then weave from that lane to the leftmost lane within a short distance (and in many cases, too short).  
Situation B - A high percentage of heavy vehicles, where in a certain direction about 15% or more (of the total traffic volume in that direction) of heavy vehicles wish to cross the intersection. Such a situation can usually occur at the entrances/exits of ports, industrial areas, large marketing and storage centers, etc. This creates a long queue of heavy vehicles in the rightmost lane, while the other lanes are not utilized to the same extent. In such a case, the element of obstruction no longer exists, so it is necessary to allow heavy vehicles to cross the intersection also in additional lane(s).  
Situation C - Entering the approach to the intersection with a left turn, from life.

In cases where the other lanes are not utilized to the same extent, there is no longer a component of obstruction, thus allowing the heavy vehicle to cross the intersection in one or more additional lanes.  
Situation C - Entering the approach to the intersection when turning left requires the heavy vehicle to maneuver and reach as soon as possible the rightmost lane, which is also the farthest lane from its entry point. Such a maneuver sometimes necessitates a very complex weaving.

 Indicates entry to a one-way street in the permitted direction of travel. As a result:

A. Traffic arrangements that include one-way streets.  
B. Increasing capacity and safety at intersections.  
C. Increasing the number of parking spaces.

1. Meaning of the traffic signs  
The beginning and end of an area where educational institutions for children of preschool, elementary school, and middle school ages are located. (See M.M. 68 in the new guidelines).  
The roads as well as the paths for bicycles and pedestrians in this area are characterized by the fact that children pass through and cross them to get to school or back home. Some move on foot by themselves, or ride on a two-wheeled vehicle, and some are transported by organized transportation in designated vehicles or by parents in private cars.  
Therefore, it is reasonable to expect pedestrian and bicycle activities among children of the aforementioned ages, as well as activities involving designated vehicles and private cars for dropping off and picking up children. This is alongside parking for residents, bus stops, and all the maneuvers involved in these activities.  
In this trend, a safety envelope for all involved, especially for the children, is required in this area, which includes slowing down and moderating traffic. Thus, it is appropriate for traffic arrangements to include speed limits of 30 km/h at most, for example, through signs 426, 426 p.  
2. Justifications for placement

1. Meaning of the markings  
The division and marking of the roadway into lanes are basic means for guiding and assisting the driver in navigating the "asphalt space," which has varying sizes and different directions of travel. This also allows for quick navigation and selection of the appropriate lane for their destination/direction of travel, thereby simplifying and reducing the variability in driving styles among different drivers and the need for frequent and confusing lane changes, which can sometimes lead to potential misunderstandings.  
For the marking to be effective and easily understood by the driver, it must be in a uniform language, simple, continuous, and hierarchical, while dividing between the different lanes and directions of travel within them according to their order of priority/importance, as follows:  
(a) Division that separates movements in opposite directions and delineates the internal roadway area – markings 801, 803, 805, 806.  
(b) Division that delineates the external roadway area – marking 807.  
(c) Division that separates movements of branching or weaving in the same direction – marking 808 (short and long rectangles).  
(d) Division that separates movements in the same direction (the basic division into lanes) – markings 801, 802, 804, 809.  
Maintaining marking according to a fixed and consistent hierarchy and method will lead over time.

(d) A division that separates movements in the same direction (the basic division into lanes) – markings 801, 802, 804, 809.  
Maintaining markings according to a fixed and consistent hierarchy and method will lead over time to quicker recognition and understanding of the way the roadway is divided and improve the driver's orientation in the "asphalt space."

1. Meaning of the traffic signs – at work sites  
The beginning and end of a work site on the road.  
They warn of work being carried out at the site (on the road and its surroundings), when workers, materials, and tools are present in the area, involving changes and/or narrowing and/or widening of the roadway or lane, to the extent of creating an obstruction to traffic flow and safety.  
In general, the marking on the road will be in orange. The marking that differs from the regular marking (in white) is meant to illustrate to the driver that the "driving environment" is different from usual, and to prompt better alertness and attention.  
Note that sign 902 at the end of the section does not cancel the restrictions and prohibitions within it.

B. Part of the road is blocked to traffic.  
C. The designation of travel lanes is different from the regular designation.

Traffic islands (in various forms), marked on the road in orange: It is forbidden to cross, stop, or park on them.

1. Meaning of the marking – at work sites  
A. Marked traffic island - in place of a built island - within the roadway that is "out of bounds" for vehicles, for any purpose, including: driving, crossing, parking, and stopping.  
B. Vehicle travel will be along the sides of the marked area - as above - according to the traffic arrangements established on site.  
2. Justifications for marking – at work sites  
A. Establishing traffic arrangements at sections and intersections which require:  
   - Defining marked separation areas between traffic lanes and paths.  
   - Creating a continuous driving flow in a manner that can be immediately perceived by drivers, allowing them to easily adapt to this continuity.  
   - Defining a hierarchy between different roads.  
   - Establishing arrangements for right and/or left turns.  
B. In general, it is preferable that various types of traffic islands be physically constructed and delineated by curbstones. In such a case, they are clear and compel the driver to act accordingly. (See in this context marking 815 regarding built traffic islands). However, in places where it is not possible to construct the island for various reasons, such as: the island area being too small, lack of lighting during dark hours, difficulties for large vehicle movement, drainage interference, etc., or at work sites where it may be required for a defined and short period, it can be painted.

It is possible to build a traffic island for various reasons, such as: the area of the island is too small, lack of lighting during dark hours, difficulties for large vehicle movement, interference with drainage, etc., or at work sites where it may be required for a defined and short period, it can be painted, as detailed here.  
Attention is drawn to the fact that a built traffic island is preferable in various ways to a marked traffic island, for example: the compliance level of drivers with a built traffic island is better, it can serve as a refuge for crossing pedestrians, a marked traffic island requires much more maintenance and it is not possible to place any signage on it.

1. Meaning of the signs – at work sites  
A barrier for vehicles on the road before places where various activities/work are being carried out, disrupting free movement.  
2. Justifications for placement – at work sites  
Before places where activities are being carried out, such as:  
- Road work.  
- Construction or infrastructure work.  
- Maintenance and repair activities.  
- Road marking.  
- Accident.  
- Blockage by the police for security and enforcement reasons.  
3. Guidelines for placement – at work sites  
A. The pole or horizontal arm will allow for blocking passage for vehicles.  
B. The pole will be made of forgiving and brittle material that will not cause damage to a vehicle that hits it – intentionally or accidentally.  
This pole is not intended to serve as a substitute for safety barriers or energy absorbers.  
C. Care should be taken to ensure good visibility of the poles and proper light reflection during dark hours.  
D. If the road is completely blocked in both directions, or if travel is only permitted in the opposite direction, a sign 401 or 402 should be placed on the barrier along with signs 205 - 204 as appropriate.  
E. If the road is partially blocked, and entry is permitted in a specific manner only, a sign 213 or 215 - 214 should be placed on the barrier.  
F. When a one-way traffic direction is established on the road, sign 618 should also be added as appropriate.

1. Meaning of the signs – at work sites  
A. A large and very prominent warning device against the general landscape. This feature is achieved from the relatively large dimensions of flashing lights with strong light intensity – even against the sun. This allows the driver to adjust their driving in advance, both in terms of the route, lane, speed, and caution.  
B. Attention to the various messages that can be derived from the board:  
   - "The road is partially closed" – but it is possible to continue driving under constrained conditions, along the route indicated by the flashing arrow and signs 215 - 213, respectively.  
   - "The road is completely closed" and there is no possibility to continue driving, as indicated by the flashing "X."  
2. Justifications for placement – at work sites  
A. At work sites where work is being carried out while traffic continues, causing disruption to the regular flow. This is especially relevant under conditions of high traffic volume and/or high speed and/or in a location that is not visible from a sufficient distance under the existing conditions. For this adaptation, one can choose one of the models presented in Column 1 of the board and in the dimensions detailed in M.M. 40, 40 A, according to the type of road, speed, and conditions at the site.  
B. The type of sign, in the format of flashing lights 932, or in the format of a projecting sign.

In this adaptation, one can choose from one of the models presented in Column 1 of the board and in the dimensions specified in M.M. 40, 40 A, according to the type of road, speed, and conditions at the location.  
B. The type of traffic sign, in the format of flashing lights 932, or in the format of a light-emitting sign, will be according to the general specifications for "flashing mobile board," published by the Land Administration / Senior Transport Planning Division (M.M. 40, 40 A).

1. Meaning of the sign – at work sites  
Indicates the existence of a stopping bay in case of emergency at a work site, at the distance specified in sign 916, which is located on road segments that do not have standard shoulders where one can stop in emergencies and distress.  
2. Justifications for placement at work sites  
A. In general, emergency stopping bays will be installed on non-urban roads (speed, primary, and regional), on the right side of the road, when the right shoulder is 3.0 m or less. The assumption is that a shoulder of this width does not allow for safe stopping.  
B. Emergency bays will be built at distances of about 2.0 km, as long as there is no exit from the road, or another option or place where stopping can be performed.  
C. In this regard, as well as the various dimensions of the bay, see in the "Guidelines for Road Design, – Volume 1, Section 3.3, Table 3.2, in the section discussing the issue of shoulder width on the road, according to the number of lanes in the cross-section. (M.M. 59).

(1) determine by notice in the official gazette the samples of traffic signs, their types, dimensions, colors, shapes, meanings, methods of placement, and marking;

Exemption for Test Conductors  
16A (a) The National Traffic Inspector may, for the purpose of conducting a test, in consultation with the licensing authority and a police officer, decide to grant an exemption to the test conductor or their representative from the provisions of one or more regulations in Chapter Two of Part B of these regulations under conditions or without conditions, as appropriate.  
(b) In making a decision under subsection (a), the National Traffic Inspector shall consider the possible impacts of conducting the test on traffic, including the following considerations:  
(1) ensuring the safety of road users during the test, including test participants.  
(2) minimizing disruption to traffic flow on roads that may be caused by conducting the test.  
(3) providing a response to emergency events that may occur during the test.  
In this regulation, "test" - the use of new technology, or a new use of technology.

In 2009-2011, the Ministry of Transportation and the Ministry of Housing launched five guideline books for street planning in cities, available in both digital and print editions. Since the distribution of these guideline books, they have served as a basis for multidisciplinary planning of streets in many new neighborhoods, for the rehabilitation of existing streets, and for the planning of streets and bike paths in master plans. The experience accumulated over nearly a decade since the launch has led the Ministry of Transportation to conduct a critical assessment of the guidelines to identify issues that require updates, refreshment, and emphasis on topics that have not been implemented, with regard to the manner of implementation thus far. 

In recent years, a policy prioritizing the development of soft mobility infrastructure (pedestrians and bicycles) and the development of public transportation infrastructure, at the expense of private vehicles, has been promoted in most advanced countries around the world. A similar development has occurred in Israel over the past decade, which included the promotion of numerous public transportation, bicycle, and pedestrian projects, at the expense of the traffic space of private vehicles and their parking areas.

Private vehicles and their parking spaces. In the field of public transportation, projects for road and rail mass transit lines are being promoted, and in a few years, several new mass transit lines will operate in various metropolitan areas. Furthermore, hundreds of kilometers of exclusive public transportation lanes are planned and being constructed. There is also significant momentum in the construction of bicycle traffic routes: in the last decade, spatial plans for bike paths have been promoted, such as "Dan Bicycles" in the Dan region and "Metropen" in the Haifa metropolitan area. Additionally, the National Transportation Infrastructure Company is promoting the development of bike paths along the main road system in Israel. Hundreds of bicycle route plans are also being advanced in cities and towns. The rapid development of transportation systems has revealed the need to update the guidelines, with a focus on updating the guidelines related to planning solutions for bicycles in street and intersection areas. Updates to standards and regulations regarding the accessibility of urban infrastructure necessitated adjustments in the guidelines. As a result, the Ministry of Transportation decided to promote the updating of the five guideline books and to prepare a new edition.

The Ministry of Transportation established a broad steering committee that included professionals from various fields. The committee held nine meetings between 2016 and 2018, during which updates to the background materials and recommendations for changes and updates were presented. Final drafts of the chapters and sections were published on the websites of the Ministries of Transportation and Housing in the summer of 2019. These were completely replaced in this edition, following the approval of the committee members and the Ministry of Transportation.

The innovations in the drafts mainly included:
- A new introduction to the planning methodology was incorporated, along with updates to street templates following the updates in the street space book that were included in other books.
- All cross-section sections were revised, and the chapter on solutions at intersections and junctions was updated (in coordination with the bicycle traffic book).
- The guidelines for public transportation stations were updated, and a section was added regarding the types of suitable paving stones for different street segments in the pedestrian traffic book.

All of these included the replacement and updating of dozens of diagrams in the various books. In the second phase, which is now concluding, all updates have been integrated into the digital edition of the five books, and they are presented to you here. Each page in this edition contains an indication of whether it has been updated. Additionally, at the beginning of each book, there is a list of changes.

Streets in cities constitute, from the perspective of the Ministry of Construction and Housing, an additional and central layer in a series of planning guidelines that the ministry has been leading in recent years in the field of sustainable development and environmentally friendly planning. The street is the main component in the planning of the urban fabric. The street space is the central field of activity in urban existence, where pedestrians, cyclists, private vehicle drivers, public transportation, and various uses that define the street coexist. All these elements merge together in a wide range of activities and interactions that are the essence of life in the city. The quality of the street is the main factor determining the quality of urban life. 

The planning of the street space and its functions aimed to primarily address the needs of private vehicles and the convenience of their drivers, while the other components and users were mainly reflected from the perspective of these needs. The new guidelines in the "Green Series" in general, and the guidelines for street planning in cities in particular, aim to balance the needs of the various users of the street space, from the perspective of all the street's functions, where the majority of human activity occurs in the urban fabric.

"The Green Line" in general, and the guidelines for street planning in cities in particular, aim to balance the needs of the various users of the street space, from a perspective of all the roles of the street, where most human activity occurs in the urban fabric. 

As with the existing guidelines, the preparation of these new guidelines was a collaboration between the Ministry of Transportation and the Ministry of Construction and Housing. The new guidelines were prepared by a multidisciplinary team that included all relevant planning fields: architecture and urban planning, traffic and transportation, roads, landscape planning and development, drainage, infrastructure planning, environmental quality, and more. 

The final product of the guidelines is a result of finding the "wise balance" between sometimes conflicting interests, between different disciplines and worldviews. We believe that these guidelines will lead to the planning of new urban fabrics and the upgrading of existing urban fabrics to be better and more friendly to all "residents" of the street who use it, while achieving the right balance between a variety of street activities, traffic flow, and safety.

The years of the State of Israel, along with various trends of population dispersion and concentration, have led to the current distribution, in which 70% of the population is concentrated in four metropolitan areas that are not as dense as most metropolitan areas in the world. Alongside them, there are urban and rural settlements in the periphery of the country. Despite all this, the State of Israel ranks high among countries where most of the population lives in cities, and thus the street, which is the artery of life, culture, and economy of the city, occupies a central and irreplaceable space in the daily existence of most citizens of the state. 

In light of this, and due to the special importance given to the street among all those engaged in the fields of engineering, behavioral sciences, and the humanities, an innovative system of guidelines for street planning was prepared about a decade ago. This system replaced previous guidelines and connected the best knowledge in Israel with the best global knowledge accumulated in the field of urban construction and architecture, integrated with the transportation sector. This was done after the government policy for land conservation and mixed-use, prioritization of public transportation, safety, and quality of life was also incorporated into the books.

The government's policy for land conservation and mixed-use, prioritizing public transportation, safety, and quality of life. The urban structure, which combines residential, employment, education, culture, and commercial uses, inherently generates significant movement of diverse populations for various purposes and between different locations. The Ministry of Transportation's policy generally states that walking is the preferred means of transportation that should be encouraged as much as possible as an alternative to motorized travel, followed by a preference for public transportation and cycling. 

First and foremost, we are pedestrians before we are drivers, and therefore a whole book in the series is dedicated to guidelines for pedestrian movement in Israel, with special emphasis on safety aspects, as the number of accidents involving pedestrians is still high, hence the effort to prevent them. 

Cycling, as an alternative to car travel, has also gained significant momentum in Israel over the past decade, aligning with sustainability. This policy states that the use of bicycles as a complementary and alternative means to private vehicles and public transportation is worthy of encouragement, as evidenced by the increasing investment in cycling infrastructure in Israel, alongside the understanding that investment in the safety of cyclists as vulnerable road users is necessary.

Looping the Ministry of Transportation's policy for private vehicles and public transportation is worthy of encouragement, as evidenced by the increasing investment in bicycle infrastructure in Israel, alongside the understanding that safety for cyclists, as vulnerable road users, must be prioritized. The update of the guidelines was requested in light of the intensive use by planners and authorities, which led to the accumulation of requests, comments, recommendations, and insights for updates and additions to the guideline books. Additionally, there has been significant progress in paving infrastructure for cyclists. In light of all the above, an updated edition of the guidelines for street planning in cities is presented to you. Special thanks to all those involved in this work, to the steering committee, to the writing team of the guidelines, and to the Senior Transportation Planning Division that promoted this important update. Most planning documents dealing with street design are two-dimensional and rarely address the third dimension - the slopes of the street plane that affect its accessibility, and the heights of street components that give it a spatial form aspect. Purpose of the Guidelines for Street Planning in Cities
A. Objective
The basic purpose of the planning guidelines is to create a guiding framework for conducting an orderly, systematic, and clear planning process, through which the policy for developing public space can be implemented as proposed in the guideline books.
The main objective guiding the guideline book before you is to enhance and improve the public space in the city, thereby contributing to shaping the city as a place that is good to live in and as a means to promote the national goal of encouraging settlement in cities.
B. Goals
To achieve the main objective, two primary goals have been defined:
• Creating safer, more efficient, accessible, and human-centered streets.
• A new allocation of public space among the various movements in the city - prioritizing "soft movements" (pedestrians and bicycles) and public transportation at the expense of private vehicle movements.
C. Means

C. Means: The means proposed by the planning guidelines document to achieve its objectives are comprehensive, controlled, and balanced planning. Coordinated, multidisciplinary planning that is attentive to all street users. The guidelines are a multidisciplinary document that provides policymakers with tools for decision-making regarding the planning, establishment, and maintenance of the street space as a whole. The guidelines present the needs of different users, the policy behind the allocation of infrastructure for them, and the perception and various planning components required for them.  
These guidelines are based on the latest guidelines and findings from countries that have already accumulated experience in developing urban space according to the new perception, while adapting them to local conditions - to the legal framework and transportation planning policy in Israel.  
Recipients of the guidelines for street planning in cities: The planning concept of the street planning guidelines is a multidisciplinary and balanced approach to street space. Therefore, all parties involved in the planning and design of public space will participate in street planning, including city planners, traffic and road planners.

C. Guidelines for bicycle movement planning in cities
The book explains the rules and guidelines for integrating bicycle movement into the urban street network of various types, so that they can move comfortably and safely alongside other street users. The guidelines are based on the assumption that bicycles are a mode of transportation that should be able to reach anywhere from anywhere, especially in the city but also outside of it. Therefore, the guidelines include measures for fully integrating bicycles within the urban framework and the city's transportation system. Bicycles are a mode of transportation, and therefore they should move separately as much as possible from pedestrians, and the level of separation from other vehicles is determined based on safety considerations. The guidelines define three levels of separation for bicycle movement (without separation) - Level A: minimal separation - in a separate lane, Level B: bicycles on the existing road, and Level C: maximum separation - on a separate path. Accordingly, the guideline book includes tools for selecting and planning the most suitable arrangement for bicycles on road segments and at intersections. The book also presents the necessary traffic signs for each arrangement and establishes the standards for bicycle parking in various uses.

A. Pedestrian Movement  
Pedestrian movement is the basic and essential component of the street and can even be the sole component (unlike an urban road). Pedestrian movement occurs along the street and must be continuous, comfortable, free of obstacles and detours, and accessible for individuals with mobility limitations. Pedestrian movement is intended to connect buildings and uses along the street and its active frontages, and therefore, complete accessibility to entrances of homes and active frontages must be maintained.  
The intensity of pedestrian movement is generally a derivative of the volume of uses along the street and their characteristics, of traffic-attracting focal points, of important locations along the street, and of the street's significance, ranking, and urban status. The greater the intensity of pedestrian movement, the more space should be allocated on the street for this movement.

Positioning strips (static strips)  
The static strips are designated areas intended to accommodate activities and uses that occur along the street but do not constitute movement along it, such as the placement of stationary objects - traffic signs and signals, light poles, barriers, street furniture, etc., vehicle parking, and space for activities along an active commercial front, and so on. The strips for stationary objects can also be shared by multiple uses and activities, provided that the shared use is reasonable and efficient, for example, using a shared strip for a tree-lined avenue, light poles, and street furniture.  
Special spaces  
Special spaces are areas required at various sections of the street or adjacent to it, often at street intersections, for local activities or uses that are not continuous, such as a bus station, a waiting area for pedestrians at crosswalks, a resting corner or other pedestrian activities, a loading and unloading area for a commercial front, space for gathering, storing, and recycling waste, and so on. Special spaces can also, under certain conditions, be shared by multiple users or be part of strips.

Street Portrait - The Program for the Street
Due to its importance, complexity, and the variety of roles of the street, its planning requires a fundamental thought process to formulate a program. The purpose of the program is to determine who and what is expected to use the street, the "strength" and scope of activity of each of the users, and to define the relationship between them. Establishing the program for the street is a prerequisite for making decisions that balance the different functions of the street and for setting priorities among them. The process of creating the program is called formulating the "Street Portrait."

The Street Portrait is a concise characterization of the planned activity in the street and its basic functions. The purpose of the 'portrait' is to allow street planners to consider the full range of considerations in the planning of the street, to intelligently balance the different needs of the users in the street, and to propose solutions for special needs of each street.

The purpose of the 'portrait' is to allow street planners to consider the full range of considerations in the planning of the street, in a reasoned manner between the different needs of the users of the street, and to propose solutions to balance the special needs of each street. In order to establish a uniform and systematic procedure for street planning in cities, a portrait will be developed for each street or segment of a street that is under planning. A street portrait will be formulated for both new streets - with regard to the concept of the street and its relative position in the planned space - and for existing streets undergoing redesign. This will be done with reference to their current functions and conditions, as well as their future roles and characteristics - as planned.

Defining the function of the street according to the proposed classification or its sub-classifications does not explicitly dictate the traffic volume within it. The street template represents an optimal balance between the needs of the users in the street and a final determination of the space allocated to each user.  
From Portrait to Template  
Introduction  
After the street portrait has been characterized, the planning team has a value program for the street. The established portrait includes the needs of the street and its urban and traffic roles, the users who will operate in the street and their relationships, structural and visual principles, and the definition of the basic infrastructure system. The portrait also includes the anchors of the portrait - rigid physical or planning dictates that serve as starting points for determining the street template.  
Determining the final template of the street - translating the values of the portrait into final quantities and dimensions - requires a deep dive into the planning guidelines for each of the street components, as detailed in the relevant guideline books - guidelines for pedestrian traffic, guidelines for bicycle traffic, guidelines for motor vehicle traffic, public transportation guidelines, and so on, as well as existing guidelines for solutions for certain streets, such as in traffic calming areas and mixed-use streets, as described in the diagram.  
Collecting the required measurements for each of the...

Bicycle traffic guidelines, motor vehicle traffic guidelines, public transportation guidelines, and similar, as well as existing guidelines for solutions for specific streets, such as in traffic calming areas and mixed-use streets, as described in the diagram. Collecting the required dimensions for each of the uses is a condition for creating the street template, but the total dimensions obtained are not necessarily the final product of the street template. It is likely that in many cases the total dimensions obtained will contradict the principles or anchors established during the portrait formulation process - for example, when the desired cross-section width exceeds the right-of-way, or when it contradicts fixed elements in the street (such as existing street trees). In such cases, it is necessary to re-examine the characteristics of the portrait, the principles formulated, and the defined anchors, and to return to the specific guidelines books to explore additional alternatives. 

It is clear, therefore, that the process of transitioning from portrait to template is a iterative process that will continue until the right and optimal balance for the specific street is found. The street template is an optimal balance between the dimensions required for each component, according to the priorities of the street and its spatial limitations.

In the typical segment plan, in addition to the linear strips, the location and rhythm of point-like recurring elements such as trees, light poles, etc., will also be described. Local solutions that will integrate into the street structure will be described, such as a typical vehicle entrance to a lot along the street, local integration of street furniture within the auxiliary strip, public transportation stations, etc.

B. Description of special segments along the street  
Unique street segments that do not characterize the linear continuity of the street and whose design is not derived from the description of the typical elements of the street will be described separately. For example - local changes in the width of the street, unusual horizontal and vertical curves, the existence of a unique object in the street space, etc. These unique segments will be described in relation to their location along the street, their geometric structure, their functioning, and how they integrate into the street continuity. For this purpose, the necessary tools will be used, such as sections or cuts that will describe the location of the linear strips, the segment plan, etc.

C. Description of the street intersections  
The design of the intersection will largely reflect how to connect the different strips in the streets meeting at the intersection. By its very nature, the intersection becomes an urban focal point, but also a point of vulnerability - both operationally and safety-wise. Therefore, the intersection will be planned separately according to a system of considerations and rules formulated for urban intersection design. This process also includes the development of a profile and template for the intersection, described in a separate book within the system - "Guidelines for Urban Intersection Design."

This is a stage of "disappointment," as in most cases there is a gap between the optimal needs required by street users and the space available to them, especially in existing streets.  
From this stage, a balancing process takes place in practice - a methodical iterative process of stages in formulating the template as faithfully as possible to the priorities, principles, and anchors established in the street profile.

Balancing the Space  
The optimal situation in which sufficient space can be allocated to each user in the street for their activity is not only impractical but largely undesirable. A clear example of this is the desire to provide a satisfactory solution for motor traffic during peak hours, a situation that creates waste of space throughout the day and even poses safety risks - an excess of traffic lanes without use encourages fast driving on one hand and careless crossing on the other hand.  
The need to save space and optimize its use requires street planners to deal with compromises and informed concessions, which can be made through the following means:  
- Informed choice to allocate in the street a reduction in the number of users requiring space allocation for their activities of specific users.

Using it requires street planners to deal with compromises and informed concessions, which can be made through the following means:
- Informed choice to allocate space on the street by reducing the number of users that require space for their activities and avoiding space allocation for other users. Examples include completely giving up a parking lane on narrow streets, giving up a lane for stationary objects on one side of the street, and relinquishing motor traffic to grant exclusivity to pedestrians on narrow streets (pedestrian zones).
- Minimizing the dimensions of the planned lanes to the reasonable minimum, even at the expense of operational efficiency. Examples include narrowing motor traffic lanes or giving up part of the traffic lanes, which reduces traffic efficiency; relinquishing a travel direction (one-way traffic only); reducing the dimensions of the lane designated for infrastructure that allows for tree planting along the street; allocating a minimal width below the width of the pedestrian lane in a way that hinders their movement, and so on.
- Creating shared spaces for multiple users, even in a way that compromises the service level of the street. Examples include a shared traffic lane for private vehicles and public transportation (a common practice in most urban areas).

In a way that burdens their movement and similar issues. - Creating shared spaces for multiple users, also in a way that compromises the sharing of spaces at the street service level. Examples - a shared traffic lane for private vehicles and public transportation (a common method in most streets); a shared traffic lane for motor vehicles and cyclists (usually requires a speed limit of 30 km/h); a shared strip for stationary objects and parking, at the cost of impacting the number of parking spaces, the number of trees, signage, and similar matters.

Templates for Existing Narrow Streets  
General Principles  
A large part of the planning tasks for urban streets in the coming years is expected to be within the existing fabric of cities as part of rehabilitation, infrastructure renewal, urban renewal, and similar initiatives. Planning within a rigid space, characterized by modest dimensions that define a large part of our streets, intensifies the competition among different space users for the allocation of space for their needs and requires delicate, meticulous, and rigorous 'tuning' to achieve an appropriate balance.  
Engagement in limited spaces necessitates compromises on minimal dimensions regarding the standards required for street users' activities, and even specific deviations that are unacceptable when planning new streets.  
Therefore, the proposed templates for existing narrow streets have been separated from those proposed for new streets. In general, variables presented for existing streets should not be adopted for new streets, except in extreme cases. For example, a one-way street should not be planned as a solution for a new street.

Minimum dimensions for strips in narrow streets:  
- The minimum width for a walking strip is 130 cm. The narrowing of the walking strip beyond this measurement is only permitted in specific cases, such as around temporary obstacles, up to 110 cm.  
- The minimum side strip for the installation of fixed objects adjacent to the side is 30 cm for thin objects like signposts and signage, or 40-50 cm for local protrusions of the built side or vegetation extending from the side line.  
- In cases of allocating a narrow side strip of 30 cm, an alternative solution must be provided for the installation of side objects such as infrastructure cabinets, etc.  
- The minimum width for a helper strip for the installation of thin fixed objects is 50 cm (with reference to the distance of the object from the curb edge and the walking strip).  
- The minimum width of a helper strip for planting trees is approximately 120 cm.

Introduction
Apart from the movements and activities occurring on the street, there are various stationary objects in the street that serve as infrastructure for street users and consumers along the street. This infrastructure is a fundamental component of the street's structure and function, enabling life and activity in the city. Environmental infrastructures, along with the use of environmental planning methods for the street, allow for the reduction of nuisances and environmental hazards and improve urban quality of life. 
However, the presence of stationary objects in the street adds an additional burden to the street space and often creates difficulties for movement and activities taking place there. Proper location and execution of the various infrastructures, along with the use of environmental planning methods, will help reduce conflicts with street users, integrate stationary objects more effectively into the street landscape, and maintain a suitable urban environment and sustainable development. 
Therefore, the policy for the installation of objects in the planned street will be determined as part of shaping the street profile and will be subject to the principles guiding the street planning and layout, as detailed in chapters 3-5, which primarily focus on establishing priorities among the various users and needs in the street.

The policy for the installation of objects in the street is planned as part of the development of a profile and will be subject to the principles guiding the design of the street and the street template (as detailed in chapters 3-5). The main focus is to establish a priority order among the various users and needs in the street (including infrastructure and stationary objects) and to ensure a balanced and controlled distribution of space according to these priorities.

The basic principles for the installation of stationary objects in the street are:
- Infrastructure components serving the street area will only include those that are required to be present there.
- The street edge will be positioned as much as possible within the boundary. For example: junction boxes, pillars, etc.
- Above the street level, only infrastructure components that are required to be above ground will be installed.
- Other infrastructure components will be underground.
- Above-ground components will only be installed in designated strips within the street (e.g., in the auxiliary strip, in the boundary strip, in separators).
- The installation of underground infrastructure will be avoided as much as possible across the width of the street.
- The installation of underground infrastructure that disrupts street activity and its characteristics will be prohibited (for example: aiming to maintain a strip free of infrastructure for tree planting).
For further details regarding above-ground and underground infrastructure in the street, see Chapter 6 "Objects and Vegetation."

Introduction  
The guidelines document for streets in cities establishes sustainable planning principles, fundamentally shifting the priority given in urban street planning to private motor vehicles, towards additional modes of transport such as pedestrians, cyclists, and public transportation. The definition of these new priorities has significant environmental implications related to reducing energy consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and other environmental aspects.  
The main objectives of sustainable development in streets are:  
- Reducing energy consumption;  
- Reducing the consumption of natural resources;  
- Minimizing negative environmental impacts;  
- Ensuring a good and healthy urban quality of life;  
- Maintaining aspects of sustainable development during the implementation stages.  
This chapter addresses two main areas in street planning:  
A. Planning considerations focused on environmental issues that impact the quality of the urban environment.  
B. Aspects of sustainable planning and development that must be taken into account during the planning and execution stages of the street.

In problematic hours and areas, there are restrictions on fuel qualities, restrictions on particularly polluting vehicles, technological improvements in vehicles, etc. Another means, although with limited effectiveness, for addressing air pollution is vegetation. Vegetation is attributed with two positive effects regarding the reduction of air pollution: 
1. The filtering effect - vegetation acts as a dust collector that helps filter it out. 
2. The shielding effect - vegetation redirects wind and dust upwards, thereby reducing concentrations at ground level. 
The filtering capacity of vegetation increases as a function of leaf area per unit of ground area, and therefore the effectiveness of vegetation as a dust collector is primarily achieved through broadleaf and evergreen trees, shrubs, and grass.

Microclimate  
The heat load in the urban street is primarily determined by three parameters:  
Temperature  
Wind intensity  
Relative humidity  
The impact of high vegetation, which creates effective shading, on the heat load in the street has been examined in studies in Israel, which reported that effective shading from vegetation in the urban street reduces the temperature by 4 degrees Celsius.  
However, it was also found that shading of the street through vegetation also creates an increase in humidity, as well as a weakening of wind intensity in the street. This shading may also create contrasts between light and shadow of up to 10% that may disturb drivers, both during the day and in lighting hours (darkness).

In terms of wind intensity on streets perpendicular to the dominant wind direction, the wind intensity is higher than on streets designed parallel to the dominant wind direction. Detention and Preservation of Stormwater  
Optimal management of stormwater in the street relates to two aspects:  
A. Detention of stormwater to prevent its arrival in large peaks (in quantity and time) to regional systems.  
B. Infiltration of stormwater into groundwater reservoirs by directing it to permeable areas and/or using permeable materials in the street.  
Detailed guidelines for optimal stormwater management are presented in the "Guide to the Preservation of Surface Stormwater" published by the Ministry of Housing.  
Environmental Compensation  
Environmental compensation is a common principle in environmental planning. This means in urban street planning that if the resulting street design includes problematic environmental quality and a high level of nuisance, environmental compensation can be proposed in another area, which will be included in the street design and improve the overall picture. For example, in a planned street where high environmental noise is present, compensation for the nuisance can be achieved by allocating space and particularly high-quality planning of vegetation to act as a barrier between traffic and noise receptors. In this way, the compensation for noise nuisances in the street will be an improvement in the experience of the user in the street.

In recent years, we have witnessed intensive development of infrastructure in general, and transportation infrastructure in particular. This development, of roads, public transportation systems, bicycle and pedestrian systems, encompasses all road networks, including urban roads. The development efforts that create infrastructure work areas, combined with the multitude of entities involved in the matter, necessitate, among other things, clear definitions regarding special and changing traffic arrangements during work, warning measures, signage, marking, and the placement of devices and materials at work sites of various types. 

These traffic arrangements, although temporary in terms of their duration of operation, are of great importance, both in terms of traffic flow and safety. This is due to the special and sometimes forced conditions that arise at work sites during the various stages of execution.

The document presented here, "Guidelines for Temporary Traffic Arrangements at Urban Work Sites," was prepared and written by a team of experts, with the writing process accompanied by a broad steering committee that included representatives from government ministries, enforcement authorities, local authorities, and private planning offices. The aim was to create a comprehensive and accurate guideline document as much as possible. This document replaces the "Guidelines for the Protection of Pedestrians on Urban Roads – 1993" and is part of a series of guidelines for traffic arrangements at work sites (alongside guidelines on this topic for intercity roads and for railway crossings, which, due to their fundamentally different characteristics from urban roads, warrant separate consideration). 

All existing guideline documents, which were prepared and written in the format of "example solutions" for various types and situations arising during work execution, and for different stages during the process, attempted to cover all situations through examples. In contrast, and in light of past experience which shows that reality, especially in the urban space, presents diverse and complex situations that cannot be predicted in advance, the new guidelines include principles, rules, criteria, and any other means that will provide the authority and its planner the ability to "build and assemble."

, primarily in the urban space,  
creates diverse and complex situations that cannot be predicted in advance. The new guidelines include principles, 
rules, criteria, and any other means that will provide the authority and its planner with the ability to "build and assemble" 
the arrangements most suitable for the conditions created at the specific work site for which the traffic arrangements are being planned. This way, planners and the local traffic authority will be able to determine the optimal arrangement according to the local conditions, rather than necessarily choosing from a catalog of examples.

In addition to the above, these guidelines emphasize the importance of addressing flow and safety issues for all road users while incorporating principles of ergonomics, particularly regarding accessibility for pedestrians and people with disabilities. This is in light of the fact that work sites present an increased risk for the latter, who must contend with a right of way that, in addition to its normal function, also accommodates the movement and operation of equipment, workers, materials, and various unusual and sometimes forced situations, unlike those typically found in areas not currently undergoing work.

On this occasion, I would like to thank all the parties who participated in writing the document, both from the office and outside of it, and especially Engineer Irit Shperber, under whose leadership most of the document was written while she served as the Director of the Senior Transportation Planning Division and as the Chair of the Steering Committee for its writing. I sincerely hope that these guidelines will bring clarity to the establishment of temporary traffic arrangements at urban work sites, as well as improve the safety of all road users in these areas, especially for the most vulnerable road users.

Chapter 1 - Introduction
1.1 Background
The State of Israel is facing a new era in which the existing transportation and infrastructure systems are on the verge of exhaustion. In the metropolitan areas: Jerusalem, Tel Aviv, and Haifa, there is a surge in the development of mass transit infrastructure: the light rail in Jerusalem, the Metronit in Haifa, and the light rail lines in the Gush Dan area. The satellite cities of the metropolitan areas are also growing, and in all cities, there is development of new basic infrastructure such as main sewage lines, drainage conduits, and water and electricity pipelines to meet the demands of natural population growth.
In addition to these infrastructures, there are urban renewal projects in older neighborhoods and street upgrades, in response to the demand arising from population growth in these cities. Over the years, dedicated infrastructures have been developed for mass transit systems above and below ground, public transportation by buses, integrated terminals, ride-sharing arrangements, bicycle paths, walking strips, and the implementation of accessibility arrangements - with additional dedicated infrastructures expected.

Accessibility - when additional dedicated infrastructures are expected. These guidelines refer to all road users both in terms of space and in terms of complementary devices. A significant difference between these guidelines and the "Guidelines for Traffic Management at Work Sites on Urban Roads" from the 1990s (referred to as the "Guide") is that the previous booklet included a series of "Principle Traffic Management Plans" (referred to as "Diagrams") that were supposed to be "representative plans" for several types of common works. In reality, it turned out that the number of work types increased and became more diverse, so the "diagrams" no longer suited (to say the least) the actual works on the ground, creating a need for adjustments and improvisations. These guidelines are updated in relation to the traffic sign schedule, regulations, and guidelines for placing traffic signs, and in relation to traffic and safety devices approved by the inter-ministerial committee. These new guidelines embed, as mentioned, a new planning approach that has shifted from a 'guide' format to a 'guidelines for the planner' format and reflects contemporary planning aspects that are compatible with the urban space in the context of all road users: pedestrians, public transport, cyclists, and private vehicles, who are the ones needing protection from the nuisances of the works, while maintaining and ensuring safety aspects.

Current planning guidelines that align with the urban space in relation to all road users: pedestrians, public transportation, cyclists, and private vehicles, who require protection from the nuisances of construction work, while maintaining and ensuring safety aspects in the vicinity of an urban work site. These guidelines emphasize providing tools for both planners and traffic authorities to establish traffic and safety arrangements at work sites in accordance with professional guiding rules that will ensure the suitability of traffic arrangements to the nature and type of work being carried out. For example, in the aspect of public transportation, the guidelines include, for the first time, extensive references and professional tools for dealing with traffic arrangements that have developed in recent years, such as bus rapid transit (BRT) systems, left-turn bus lanes, traffic signal priority, and light rail construction, including tunneling and earthworks that require the transportation of materials to and from the site. These guidelines also address the planning of temporary traffic arrangements for roundabouts and multi-lane intersections. Chapter 2 – Design Principles  
Guidelines for Planning Temporary Traffic Arrangements at Urban Work Sites  
Chapter 2 - Design Principles  
2.1 Background  
This chapter presents the geometric traffic planning principles for designing temporary traffic arrangements. When carrying out infrastructure work in the urban space, consideration must be given to the nature of the area where the activity is taking place. It is essential to plan in a way that maintains pedestrian and cycling routes, alongside preserving capacity and service levels on travel lanes.  
Short-term work in residential neighborhoods will typically be conducted during the day, while in business and commercial areas, it will be carried out at night to minimize disruption to normal life.  
Carrying out work at night is subject to the provisions of regulations for preventing nuisances – noise prevention – and requires special permits that are granted sparingly by the heads of local authorities.

2.1.1 Work Site Planning  
The work site organization plan from a safety perspective is defined in the Safety Regulations for Construction Work, 1988.  
Safety requirements for interfaces between work sites and adjacent roads are found in Chapter 9 of the guidelines (highlights and special cases).  
The contractor's organization area is required in cases of short-term and long-term work, in infrastructure and development work, and in engineering construction work. In some cases, construction materials are stored in parking bays or on sidewalks, partially narrowing them. Sometimes these construction materials remain on site for several days and require fencing and separation from the built environment, along with appropriate traffic arrangements.

2.2.2 Path Balancing and Preservation of Walking/Cycling Routes  
In general, at work sites in urban areas, sidewalks and walking paths should be kept open on both sides of the road, especially during prolonged works. For short-term works, it is permissible to block the walking path of pedestrians*, but it is recommended to place a traffic sign/guide in the blocking areas. The placement of the traffic sign/guide is recommended to ensure the safe passage of pedestrians in a controlled manner near engineering machinery.  
Blocking sidewalks and bike paths is not allowed near public institutions in general and schools in particular at the beginning and end of operating hours.  
Blocking sidewalks and bike paths is sometimes not feasible on urban roads with high traffic volumes and actual driving speeds of over 50 km/h. Transferring bicycle or pedestrian traffic from one side of the road to the other creates a risk and a lack of willingness to comply from pedestrians.  
In ongoing works, sidewalks for pedestrians and bike paths should be preserved on both sides of the road. In wide streets and during peak hours, there is low willingness among pedestrians and cyclists to move to opposite sidewalks due to heavy traffic congestion and the difficulty of crossing at unregulated intersections or, alternatively, due to long waiting times at traffic lights.

Roadway.  
In wide streets and during peak hours, there is a low willingness among pedestrians and cyclists to switch to opposite sidewalks due to heavy traffic congestion and the difficulty of crossing at unregulated intersections or, alternatively, due to long waiting times at regulated intersections (due to cycle length).  
In cases of sidewalk blockage, the blockage should be planned in a location that allows pedestrians and cyclists to access alternative routes that enable comfortable and uninterrupted passage. Blocking a sidewalk in the middle of a segment is undesirable since pedestrians and cyclists will always prefer the shortest route, even if it requires walking in the travel lane.  
Sometimes, street closures are required during construction work. The planner's awareness of different execution methods will greatly influence traffic arrangements. For example, there are casting methods that allow concrete to be transported over distances that enable the placement of the pump in a location where travel lanes do not need to be blocked.  
When the available roadway allows a minimum lane width of 2.75 m, traffic can be directed in a "stop and go" format. Otherwise, other options should be examined, and only if there is no alternative should the street be closed to traffic and redirected to a detour.

Traffic can be redirected in a "stop and go" format for 5 meters. Otherwise, alternative options should be examined, and only if there is no choice should the street be closed to traffic and redirected to a detour.

2.2.4 Maximum Allowed Speed  
The basic design policy of a work site is based on the concept that if it is not necessary to reduce the maximum allowed speed (MAS), it should not be reduced. The goal is to strive for a balance between design speed, maximum allowed speed, and operational speed (the speed at which drivers are observed traveling under free flow conditions). The systemic view of managing travel speeds at the work site will determine the "Target Speed" (the desired travel speed on a defined type of road). The target speeds for different types of work are determined based on a broad consideration mechanism, primarily aimed at maintaining mobility and ensuring the safety of road users.  
The maximum allowed speed in the work area will be determined based on the maximum allowed speed prior to the commencement of work. In these guidelines, the maximum allowed speed refers to the maximum allowed speed that exists before the work begins unless stated otherwise, and the speed due to the work is derived from it.  
From the perspective of the road user, this is a speed that is suitable for traveling on a specific road, which the design of the road and its surroundings are supposed to convey. The aspiration is that despite lane narrowing (when it is implemented), most vehicles will travel freely at a speed close to the maximum allowed speed.

The road user, this is a speed that is suitable for traveling on a specific road, which the road design and its surroundings are supposed to convey. The aspiration is that despite lane narrowing (when it is implemented), most vehicles will travel freely at a speed close to the designated speed.

2.2.5 Determining Operating Hours  
The determination of operating hours within the built environment is often influenced by the policy of the local authority and by the provisions of [the Prevention of Nuisances Law, 1961, and the regulations for preventing nuisances] – [Noise Prevention, 1992].  
Carrying out work during lighting hours (night) requires obtaining approval from the head of the local authority for deviations from the provisions of the law and regulations.  
Nighttime work is met with dissatisfaction from residents due to the disruption of normal life. Performing work during the day has advantages in residential neighborhoods. Parking is often available on one-way or multi-lane roads.

2.3.2 Minimum Width for Pedestrian Passage  
The planning of pedestrian movement at urban work sites must be done with the recognition that the urban space is a space for pedestrians, and therefore it is necessary to ensure safe and comfortable passage for pedestrians.  
The walking route must be arranged during the execution of the work, even at the cost of creating localized disruptions in the roadway used for motor vehicles.  
The extent of pedestrian activity on the street is a significant parameter in determining the type of solution. There is a basic distinction between providing solutions for pedestrians on local roads where pedestrian presence is often sparse, compared to work being carried out on streets with commercial fronts in the city center.  
The work site should be characterized in relation to the extent of pedestrian activity and in relation to the adjacent land uses such as: schools and hospitals, rehabilitation institutions, and nursing homes.  
The maximum period is examined according to the execution phase, meaning, for a development project lasting 3 years and based on 3 execution phases of one year each, it is required to plan the temporary traffic arrangements and the walking strip while complying with the requirements of the planning guidelines and standard 1918, for a permanent arrangement.

In general, the aim is to preserve the walking route on both sides of the road. In cases where it is not possible to meet the minimum values stated in table 2.3.6, the cancellation of a travel lane should be considered. In such cases, closing a travel lane allows for the creation of a detour for pedestrians without the need to transfer them to the opposite sidewalk. In cases where it is not possible to cancel a travel lane, and the width of the pedestrian passage does not allow for compliance with the minimum values, the walking route should be blocked, and pedestrians should be directed to the opposite sidewalk. In this situation, the design will include traffic arrangements with a safe pedestrian crossing, and the walking route on the opposite sidewalk should accommodate pedestrians. Additionally, the design should include the possibility of returning to the original walking route later on. 

When planning the width of the walking strip, it is necessary to incorporate the entire range of street furniture and facilities such as: bicycle racks, guide rails, bus stops, etc. The pedestrian strip should be continuous and free of obstacles.
