2.3.5.3      Work on Sidewalks / Paths / Bicycle Lanes  
When carrying out any work, the width of the work site is equal to the width of the sidewalk. For this reason, performing work on the sidewalk requires directing pedestrians to an alternative sidewalk. This direction will be made at the last decision point that allows for a transition to an alternative sidewalk.  
Blocking a path / bicycle lane or sidewalk in the middle of a section is undesirable, as in such situations pedestrians may bypass the work site through the travel lanes. Pedestrians and cyclists will generally choose the shortest route (naturally). For this reason, an alternative (detour) route must be arranged alongside the site without transferring pedestrians to the opposite sidewalk. This solution is essential on two-lane roads, where pedestrians, in most cases, will not cross to the opposite sidewalk due to crossing distances and the need to cross the road again later.  
In urban areas, there is continuity of activity along the sides, such as businesses, residences, etc. Transferring pedestrians to the opposite sidewalk can create situations where pedestrians and cyclists are forced to turn back to reach their destination.  
For all the reasons mentioned above, a passage for pedestrians must be created alongside the work site. Transferring to the opposite sidewalk will be, as

The sidewalk across the street can create situations where pedestrians and cyclists are forced to turn back to reach their destination. For all the reasons mentioned above, a pedestrian crossing must be created on the side of the work site. Transferring to the sidewalk across the street will, as stated, be the last option to choose. Similarly, when work is being carried out along bike paths and lanes, they need to be blocked due to their width. In these cases, an appropriate solution must be provided for cyclists to avoid diverting them from their intended destination. A separation between motor traffic and pedestrian movement must be implemented, depending on the speed of the road and the duration of the work. If the duration of the work is short (up to 12 hours) and the speed is not high (30 km/h), light fencing is sufficient for separation. If the speed is high or the duration of the work is long, it is necessary to install an appropriate safety railing. *See Figure 4.6 in Chapter 4 for these guidelines.

2.3.6 Work at Intersections  
Work at intersections differs in nature from work on road segments, as it affects multiple directions of travel simultaneously. Blocking intersections is only permissible when there are available detours. Signage and guidance for drivers along the route is required, including notification signs for turns at intersections along the route.  
In cases where partial closure of the intersection is necessary, lane closures or narrowing should be implemented before the point where turning lanes open, according to the principle of lane closures on road segments. The area of the intersection is considered from the point where turning lanes open or, in the absence of turning lanes, from a measured distance of 12 meters from the tangent to the radius of the intersection (the point where the radius of the curb stones begins). However, work near the intersection can affect traffic arrangements at the intersection and may sometimes require prior attention and signage before the turn.

Blocking routes is sometimes required for short-term activities, such as grinding and resurfacing work and public events like competitions or parades. 2.9 Fences, Safety Barriers, and Additional Devices  
Introduction  
The need for protection in urban areas arises from the fact that construction sites on urban roads are located near pedestrian, bicycle, and other road users, and sometimes even affect their movement.  
Marking or delineating a work area is intended to indicate and separate the activity area from road users and to protect them from the dangers present in the work area. The marking or delineation can be done between the site and the active traffic lanes or between the site and the sidewalk/bicycle path.  
The marking or delineation highlights the location of the work and creates a physical barrier that helps to emphasize the location of the site and to alert about the location of work within or near the road.

3.1 Existing Street Lighting  
Traffic arrangements at work sites in cities must include lighting for safety reasons in accordance with the applicable guidelines for road lighting installation.  
The existing road lighting sometimes serves as a basis for lighting at the site, even when work is being carried out. To rely on it, it must be integrated and marked in the plans; the road lighting must be functional and comply with all relevant guidelines before the work begins.  
3.2 Lighting at Temporary Work Sites on Urban Roads  
On roads and streets where temporary traffic arrangements exist, road lighting should be planned according to the "Guidelines for Planning Road Lighting" in effect, and the lighting intensity should comply with the guidelines.  
• Road lighting must be arranged at every work site.  
• The guidelines for planning road lighting define the required intensity of road lighting in urban areas.  
• If there is a desire to rely on the existing street lighting, its functionality must be checked before the work begins and marked in the temporary traffic arrangements.  
• The lighting intensity should be examined according to the guidelines in the area of the site before the activity begins and regularly every week.

If there is a desire to rely on the existing street lighting, its condition must be checked before the start of the work and marked with temporary signs. 
• The intensity of the lighting should be examined according to the guidelines in the area of the site before the start of the activity and on an ongoing basis every week (visual inspection). 
• In the absence of existing street lighting on an urban road where work is required, street lighting must be installed at all stages of execution, with an intensity that meets the requirements of the guidelines for lighting design on roads. 
• The location of lighting poles on an urban road will be adjusted to the components of the cross-section as will be described later.

3.3 Differences in Typical Lighting Intensities in Work Areas  
At every site where work is conducted at night, there will be a lighting consultant as part of the work team, whose role is to plan the road lighting on the roads while considering various factors that may affect the work environment, such as:  
- Adjacent areas illuminated with high intensity, such as stadiums or shopping centers, which may cause glare and disturbance.  
- Various work sites alongside the road that have their own lighting means for the work, even in proximity to active travel lanes.  
The lighting at the site must comply with the standard lighting level according to the road level and not just the existing lighting level. This is because the traffic arrangements at a work site are forced, and it is necessary to compensate for this with standard lighting.  
The lighting at the site should not glare at different road users and should be planned according to the guidelines for road lighting design.

4.1 Pedestrian Safety in Temporary Traffic Arrangements  
Temporary traffic arrangements must be designed so that the movements of pedestrians, cyclists, and public transportation activities are maintained in their regular form, without compromising their level of service and physical conditions. This may come at the expense of private vehicle traffic.  
Similarly, safety aspects should be prioritized over capacity and service level for motor vehicles. One of the primary measures for safety in traffic arrangements will include, among other things, a significant and gradual reduction of the speed limit, actual travel speed, reduction in the number of lanes, and the establishment of enforced geometry that requires careful and controlled driving.  
Sidewalks for pedestrian movements should protect them from disturbances caused by the forced street conditions and the works being carried out nearby. Accordingly, a walking strip should be reserved for pedestrians, with an appropriate width according to Table 2.3.6, free from objects, obstacles, and facilities in general, and specifically due to the ongoing works.

In short-term work (lasting from 30 minutes to 12 hours, conducted on a daily basis and with the site being closed at the end of the activity), pedestrian access to the road must be prevented due to sidewalk blockage. In ongoing work, it is possible to direct pedestrians to the road using a temporary ramp or another means, provided there is a separation from the traffic lanes. The walking strip must be maintained even at the expense of private vehicle parking space, and physical barriers should be used to prevent vehicle parking on the sidewalk, due to the impact on the walking area. A temporary traffic arrangement that allows shared movement (between pedestrians and cyclists) is not permitted, even in cases where a nearby bike path has been canceled. Such a case will only be allowed if the sidewalk is wide enough to allocate a lane or path for bicycles.

4.7 Sidewalk Accessibility  
A temporary walking strip should be designed to allow mobility for various users on the street: for pedestrians, especially for those with difficulties such as: children, the elderly, strollers, and people with limited mobility (disabled). An accessible path will be planned as required by standard 1918 part 1 section 2.7.  
In all arrangements for pedestrians, on sidewalks, in walking strips, and especially at connections between them, attention must be paid to the details.

Bicycles are an accessible and efficient means of transportation in urban areas. To carry out work on bicycle paths, it is necessary to prepare a temporary traffic plan accordingly, in order to provide a safety response. Bicycles and other light two-wheeled vehicles such as scooters can reach high speeds (sometimes 30 km/h), and the level of risk for users and those around them is relatively high. Therefore, arrangements should prioritize separation between bicycle paths and motor vehicle traffic on one side and pedestrian walkways on the other side.  
The determination of traffic arrangements for bicycle paths and/or bicycle lanes will be based on the principles established in previous chapters. The purpose of this chapter is to complete special emphasis on bicycle movements and the different sensitivities of two-wheeled vehicles compared to motor vehicles.

In the case of a bidirectional bike path that is blocked due to road work, the handling of the arrangement will be divided into two parts:  
A. Cyclists traveling in the direction of traffic will be integrated into the travel lanes. This rule applies to streets with a maximum permitted speed of up to 50 km/h, before the start of the work. For roads, cyclists should be redirected to alternative routes and the path should be closed at the intersection closest to the site.  
B. Cyclists traveling against the direction of traffic will not be directed to the travel lanes. For them, the path should be blocked at the nearest intersection and they should be directed through pedestrian crossings so that they can merge into the travel lanes in the direction of their travel.  
In the case of a road with a maximum speed of over 50 km/h before the work is carried out, cyclists should be redirected to an alternative route and not merged with the motor vehicle traffic in their direction of travel.  
For short-term work on bike paths, such as work on electrical or telecommunications trenches, cyclists traveling in the direction of traffic are required to merge into the vehicle travel lane or dismount and walk on the sidewalk. Cyclists traveling against the direction of traffic are required to cross the road at the nearest pedestrian crossing to the work site and continue their journey on the bike path or sidewalk opposite.
Bicyclists are required to cross the road at the nearest crosswalk to the work site and continue their ride on the bike path/sidewalk opposite.

Chapter 11 – Procedure for Submitting Plans to the Traffic Authorities  
Guidelines for Planning Temporary Traffic Arrangements at Urban Work Sites  
The purpose of this procedure is to establish a uniform basis for submitting plans for temporary traffic arrangements for approval, with the intention of creating consistency in the preparation, presentation, and approval of traffic arrangement plans by the traffic authority.  
11.1 Planner's Approval of Compliance with Planning Guidelines  
Every plan for temporary traffic arrangements at work sites on urban roads submitted for approval must include the planner's signature confirming that the plan complies with legal requirements, regulations, standards, and planning guidelines. In the case of changes to traffic lights, this signature must be on both the engineering arrangement plan and the timeline plan. Additionally, the following must be highlighted on the plan:  
- Name of the planner, their registration number in the civil engineering field, name of the planning office, and its details.  
- Name of the plan, its number, edition number, and update date.  
- General description of the plan and its principles (for example: considerations for pedestrians, traffic diversions, and changes to bus stops), planning and placement of temporary lighting, diversion of systems, presentation of how to arrange temporary and permanent accessibility, etc.  
- General description of the phases of execution and duration of execution of

Reference to pedestrians, traffic diversions, and changes at bus stops, planning and placement of temporary lighting, system deviations, presentation of the method for arranging temporary and permanent accessibility, and so on.  
- General description of the phasing of execution and the duration of each phase in projects with multiple execution stages.  
The wording of the planner's commitment will be:  
"I hereby confirm that the submitted plan for approval was prepared by a licensed engineer and complies with the guidelines of the national traffic supervisor, the valid traffic signs, and legal requirements."  
If necessary, the planner may add an appendix to the plan containing additional details not specified in the plan itself. In such a case, a reference to the appendix will be indicated on the plan accordingly.  
11.2 Temporary traffic arrangements in urban road work sites.

The plan will be based on a map that reflects the existing traffic arrangements at the time of preparing the plan, particularly the traffic signs placed in the area. The background map can be one of the following alternatives (see also illustrations 11.2, 11.3, and 11.4 below):
- Detailed measurement for planning - intended for geometric changes as well.
- Photogrammetric measurement - these plans will only be prepared as environmental diagrams, such as guidance for detours.
- Aerial photograph - can serve as a background only when the resolution is sufficient and there is no coverage that impairs the ability to reproduce the traffic arrangements.

The book "Guidelines for Planning Motor Vehicle Traffic in Cities" is the fourth book in the series of guideline books for street planning in cities. While the previous books in the series focused on the soft users of the street, pedestrians and cyclists, this book addresses motor vehicle drivers of various types, as well as the characteristics and "heavy" functional requirements of the vehicles themselves.  
This book discusses the geometric design of the street, focusing on components related to motor vehicles, which generally occupy the majority of land allocation on the street. These components include the roadways with their various characteristics and widths, intersections and traffic islands, and the issue of parking, a significant component whose presence greatly influences the street's profile and the nature of the urban space as a whole.  
The current book addresses typical street segments that actually represent most of the street's length, focusing on the characteristics and events occurring within them, while concurrently, a book discussing urban intersections and their surroundings is being published.  
In this book, the components of geometric design have been updated, reflecting the worldview characteristic of the five guideline books in the series, according to which the geometry of the street dictates and determines the behavior of street users in general, and drivers in particular.

The concept underlying the guidelines  
These guidelines for motor vehicle traffic in cities are part of a series of new guideline books for urban street planning, as will be described in the following sections. As explained in the master book of the series - "Planning the Street Space," these guidelines represent a new and more balanced worldview compared to the planning concepts that were prevalent in the second half of the 20th century, which prioritized the 'street for vehicles' concept - the capacity and level of service for private vehicles, as the main planning goal.  
This concept has significantly influenced the direction of the street's other roles and urban planning, which have become less and less inviting and safe for other road users. Since the end of the 20th century, there has been a global aspiration to halt the decline of urban space. In many places around the world, it has been understood that the desire to provide city residents with immediate access by private vehicle to every destination is questionable in terms of long-term feasibility, but its cost in terms of quality of life and well-being is already unreasonable.  
Therefore, the new guideline books for urban street planning are based on a new and more balanced worldview - largely more traditional (and perhaps even more biblical), grounded in several fundamental principles:  
A. A good street is a street that is good for people present.

The new guidelines for urban street planning are based on a new and more balanced worldview - largely more traditional (and perhaps even more biblical), founded on several fundamental principles:
A. A good street is one that is good for the people who are in it.
B. The street space has many and varied roles - systemic, visual, social, and others.
C. The street space should provide an efficient and economical response to all activities taking place within it.
D. Street planning requires a controlled and balanced allocation of street space among all its users.
E. The quality of the street depends on and influences the quality of the entire fabric related to it.
Within this framework of reallocating street space among all its users, private and commercial vehicles must also find their place in a balanced and fair mix with pedestrians, cyclists, public transport, and other users. The guidelines before you detail the planning principles for the traffic and parking lanes allocated on urban streets for motor vehicles, after previous books dedicated to planning for pedestrians and bicycles.

After the previous books dedicated to planning for pedestrians and bicycles, the following emphasizes the new guidelines for street planning in cities, detailed in section 1.3, which place safety, quality of life, and consideration for the desires of residents and the community at the top of the priority list in urban environment and transportation infrastructure planning.

The purpose of the guidelines for street planning in cities is to create a guiding framework for conducting an orderly, systematic, and clear planning process, through which the policy for developing public space can be implemented as proposed in the guideline books.

The guidelines are a multidisciplinary document that provides policymakers with tools for decision-making regarding the planning, establishment, and maintenance of the street space as a whole. The guidelines present the needs of various users, the policy behind the allocation of infrastructure for them, and the concepts and different planning components required.

These guidelines are based on the latest guidelines and findings from countries that have already accumulated experience in developing urban space according to the new concept, while adapting them to local conditions - to the legal framework and planning policy.

Bicycle Traffic  
The first guideline book on this topic in Israel. The book explains the rules and guidelines for integrating bicycle traffic into the urban street network of various types, so that they can move comfortably and safely alongside other street users. The guidelines are based on the assumption that bicycles are an accepted mode of transportation that should be able to reach anywhere from anywhere, especially in the city but also outside of it. Therefore, the guidelines include measures for fully integrating bicycles within the urban framework and the city's transportation system. Bicycles are a mode of transport, and thus they should move separately as much as possible from pedestrians, with the level of separation from other vehicles determined by safety considerations. The guidelines define three levels of separation for bicycle traffic:  
- Level A (no separation) - integration of bicycle traffic with motor vehicles,  
- Level B (minimal separation) - in a separate lane alongside motor traffic lanes,  
- Level C (maximum separation) - in a separate path.  
Accordingly, the guideline book includes tools for selecting and planning the most suitable arrangement for bicycles on road segments and at intersections. The book also presents the necessary traffic signs for each arrangement.

The basis of the planning concept for the set of guidelines for street planning and its various derivatives is a multidisciplinary and balanced approach to the street space. Therefore, all parties involved in the planning and design of the public space will participate in street planning, including urban planners, traffic and road planners, architects, landscape and environmental planners, infrastructure planners, and others. In addition to all these, the book is directed at decision-makers and policymakers, representatives of stakeholders in the public space, and even the general public. The wide variety of consumers of the planning guidelines presents a challenge in the formulations of the book and its definitions. This is with the aspiration to be as clear and transparent as possible to the broad target audience, without losing the professional accuracy required in each field. By necessity, there will be sections in the guidelines written in language more understandable to a 'non-professional audience,' and other sections with a more professional tone, addressing urban planning, transportation planning, landscape planning, physical infrastructure, and additional topics from various professional fields. It is therefore recommended for anyone involved in street planning to review and familiarize themselves, in addition to the guidelines in their area of expertise, with the basic guidelines detailed in the book "Street Space," which serves as the 'parent book' of the "Guidelines for Street Planning in Cities," as well as to familiarize themselves as much as possible with the professional guidelines related to parallel planning fields. 

The scope of flexibility in applying the guidelines for street planning
The guidelines present the planner with the options available to them. However, the guidelines are not intended to limit the planner's solutions but rather to define a framework on one hand and to broaden their horizons on the other hand, in order to assist them in dealing with non-standard problems. The proposed set of guidelines includes basic definitions of key policies and planning principles on various issues, as well as a wide range of specific guidelines, design details, computational methods, recommended and minimum dimensions, and so forth. The aim of these is primarily to provide planning and thinking tools, as well as to...

Fundamentals of key policies and planning principles on various topics, as well as a wide range of specific guidelines, design details, computational methods, recommended and minimum dimensions, and so forth. The primary aim of these is to provide planning and thinking tools, as well as to inspire and encourage the planner in searching for the most suitable solutions for the specific case at hand. There is no doubt that the proposed set of guidelines does not provide answers to all future planning challenges, but rather a partial response to the more common and familiar cases. Most planning tasks generate local and unique problems, the solutions to which will require significant effort, creativity, judgment, and decisions from the planning team. In any planning challenge, it is highly recommended to rely on the worldview, policies, and planning principles presented in the guidelines, such as a comprehensive view of public space, a detailed examination of the needs of users, a controlled balance of space allocation, planning for maximum safety (and less for maximum capacity), and so forth.

The general concept of speed planning and management
Speed is one of the basic characteristics of traffic flow, defining the flow state at both the macro and micro levels. High speed on a road indicates good flow conditions, both as a result of road data and traffic data. On the other hand, from a safety perspective, most studies indicate a correlation between speed and the occurrence and severity of traffic accidents, with the variance in speeds among different vehicles also contributing to road insecurity.
How to adapt: Therefore, the central issue when dealing with speed in the street is to determine the appropriate speed that meets operational, safety, economic, social, and other needs, as there is an inherent contradiction among them.
The solution lies in establishing a priority order of needs for each street. Subject to this, appropriate travel speeds for each street will be determined, and as a result, the geometric characteristics required by this speed.
The speed of vehicle movement on the street has a direct impact and connection to other users, the rate of crosswalks, the existence of medians and the type of medians, the presence or absence of: for example, parking lanes.

They are intended to facilitate traffic flow from area to area in the metropolitan urban arterial road network. There should be an aspiration to plan at a high traffic standard, so that these roads will carry the majority of traffic and provide high capacity at a reasonable level of service. The design should reflect the fact that the permitted speeds on these roads should be relatively high compared to the rest of the urban network. The level of safety on these roads will not be compromised, as long as they are designed for a high level of safety, taking into account the fact that there are very vulnerable road users (pedestrians, cyclists, light motorcycle riders), whose bodies cannot withstand the consequences of an accident occurring at 70 km/h. One of the main means of maintaining a high level of safety at this speed is to create maximum separation on the roads between vulnerable users and the rest of the motor traffic. In the urban system, the collector and local streets are primarily intended for traffic flow.

In the urban system, the collector and local streets are primarily designated for accessibility purposes. These streets must reflect their lower traffic status in the network, both in geometric standards and in permitted speeds. The lower traffic status of these streets for through traffic, and their primary function for accessibility, will redirect through traffic to higher-level streets that are designed for that purpose. Therefore, safety will increase not only on urban roads but throughout the entire urban network. 

Additionally, in the urban system, there are traffic-calmed streets where the design perception is different, meaning that low speed is not achieved by placing traffic signs, but through special traffic arrangements and engineering and architectural measures. The management of travel speeds on the street network should be based on a single systemic rationale. As a first step in this process, a clear definition of the roles of the streets in the network is required - a hierarchy of streets. The hierarchy of streets is determined considering the topographical structure, population concentrations, transportation needs, statutory considerations, and especially considering mobility considerations, traffic transfer and flow, traffic distribution, or access to residential areas. For each type of street, a physical space for establishment (right of way) and design principles are defined. The systemic view of managing travel speeds on the street network requires that for each type of street, a desired travel speed is defined - "design speed." The designation for different types of streets is determined according to a variety of considerations including mobility, safety, environmental quality, quality of life in population concentrations, and more, which are examined at the systemic level (of the entire road network). Types of Speed in the Planning Process
Target speed is the desired travel speed on the street, which has specific planning characteristics. In the eyes of the street user, the planning characteristics of the streets and their surroundings are supposed to 'signal' what the appropriate speed is.

Speed in the planning process refers to the desired travel speed on the street, characterized by target speed specifications. In the eyes of the street user, the design characteristics of the streets and their surroundings should 'signal' what the appropriate speed for traveling on the street is. The aspiration is that most vehicles on this type of street will travel at a speed close to the target speed.

The maximum speed limit is the maximum speed allowed for drivers to travel on this street under normal traffic and weather conditions, according to traffic regulations or the posted sign.

Design speed is the speed determined for the purpose of the geometric design, establishing the geometric characteristics that affect vehicle operation with maximum safety. 

The planning process is carried out as follows:

The traffic function of the street is not disconnected from the urban role of the street, but it does not necessarily overlap with it. The urban significance of the street does not necessarily overlap with its traffic role. Urban roads play a crucial traffic function, but their direct urban importance is very small and sometimes even problematic. Restrictions on pedestrian activity along the road turn it into a 'repellent space' along its length. Local streets with minimal vehicle traffic often have low urban significance (small residential streets, etc.), but it is also important to pay attention to the opposite phenomena - local streets that are marginal in terms of traffic but have special urban importance (Shenkin Street in Tel Aviv).

Such a collector street is characterized by a richness of activity that exceeds the importance of the residential uses along it and serves a population from a larger area, necessarily resulting in a greater volume of movements for a variety of users.

Separators - Their Roles and Types  
The separator is a strip within the street that divides different vehicle movements and opposing directions of traffic. The separator has many diverse roles in street planning, as detailed below:  

Roles related to motor vehicle traffic in the street:  
A. To serve as a safety barrier between different vehicle movements, in the same direction or in opposing directions (including bus lanes, bicycles, etc.).  
B. To guide and direct drivers within intersections and to provide optional space for creating special lanes for left turns.  
C. To moderate the nature of traffic in the street.  
D. An engineering tool for traffic management (preventing left turns, U-turns, etc.).  

Roles related to infrastructure and stationary objects:  
A. To provide a suitable location for placing road facilities and infrastructure such as lighting poles, signage, and barriers.  
B. To contribute to the visual landscape of the street by planting trees and other vegetation along its length.  

Roles related to pedestrian traffic and activity:  
A. To improve the safety of crossing the road for pedestrians and to serve as a refuge for them.  
B. In a boulevard - to serve as the "heart" of the street.  

This distinction between the different (and even conflicting) roles of the separator is very important. The decision to install a separator in the street must be accompanied by a clear definition of its purpose.

Introduction
A "dead-end street" is a regular urban street that is similar in all its components to those of urban streets, but is distinguished from them by the fact that the entry into it by motor vehicles from the surrounding area is also the only exit from it back to that area.
The natural and preferred tendency in urban and transportation planning is to create a street that has at least two connection points to its surrounding area for motor vehicles. However, sometimes, for various urban and engineering reasons, there is no choice but to create a "dead-end street."
It should be emphasized that the absence of an exit for vehicles does not necessitate the absence of an exit for pedestrians and bicycles. On the contrary, the more continuity and connectivity of the pedestrian network is ensured, the better its quality will be, and it will guarantee greater usage. Therefore, if necessary, it is advisable to allow multi-directional movement for pedestrians and bicycles even on streets that are dead ends for motor vehicles.
In such cases, it is common to designate "dead-end streets" primarily in residential areas, which rely on private vehicle traffic spread throughout the day, and to avoid, as much as possible, designating them next to uses that attract large traffic volumes.

In such cases, it is common to designate "dead-end streets" primarily in residential areas, based on private vehicle traffic spread throughout the day, and to avoid, as much as possible, placing them next to uses that attract large traffic volumes during short time periods, such as schools, clusters of kindergartens, cinemas, theaters, etc. In such cases, vehicles block the street and disrupt both the external traffic continuing to the street and the local traffic wishing to exit during these times. It is also recommended to avoid designating "dead-end streets" next to industrial uses and uses that attract trucks and buses, as these vehicles will require significant expansion of several street components, especially the turning area.

The stopping sight distance is the sum of two components - the perception-reaction distance and the braking distance. The perception-reaction distance is the distance the vehicle travels during the time from the moment of detecting an obstacle until the brakes are activated; the perception time is the time that elapses from the moment of detecting the obstacle until the decision to apply the brakes, and the reaction time is the time that elapses from the moment of the decision to apply the brakes until the actual braking begins. The braking distance is the distance the vehicle travels from the moment the brakes are applied until it comes to a complete stop. Over the years, the braking systems of modern vehicles have significantly improved, increasing the deceleration capability and improving braking distances. At high speeds on wet surfaces, most vehicles can decelerate at 2 m/s². On dry surfaces, most drivers can decelerate at rates exceeding 4.5 m/s² before encountering an object that is not anticipated. The deceleration parameter has become the dominant parameter for determining the braking distance, due to the ABS (Anti-lock Braking System) systems installed in most vehicles, which ensure deceleration without the risk of wheel lockup.

Side Elevation in Horizontal Curves
Needs and Limitations
Changes in direction in the horizontal alignment are made by designing circular arcs between the straight sections. In the circular arcs, a centrifugal force acts on the vehicle, pushing it outward from the curve. This force is balanced by a lateral friction factor that develops between the wheels and the pavement, as well as by a side elevation of the pavement, with a uniform slope greater than that of the normal crown. 
From a traffic perspective, it is preferable to provide side elevations in horizontal curves, thereby reducing dependence on lateral friction; however, in urban areas, there are several constraints that make it very difficult or undesirable to change the normal crown of the pavement. Among the various factors limiting the provision of elevation, the following factors exist:
Generally, the drainage of urban streets is through underground drainage, A. Drainage of the pavement, with the inlets located near the curb stones. Therefore, if the drainage line runs along the right curb stone, a side elevation in the opposite direction will transfer the water across the pavement to the median or to the opposite curb stone. Although this problem can be solved engineering-wise.

The collectors are located near the curb stones. Therefore, if the drainage line runs along the right curb stone, a lateral elevation in the opposite direction will direct the water across the roadway to the median or to the opposite curb stone. Although this issue can be solved through engineering, the planner must carefully consider the drainage problems in the elevated section. 

Urban streets are characterized by the presence of many intersections. The processing of heights at intersections along the streets, as well as entrances for side uses, is significant. Therefore, when there is a horizontal curve, or immediately adjacent to it, if there is an intersection, providing lateral elevation may complicate the proper arrangement of slopes and heights at the intersection.

Urban streets provide high accessibility to adjacent land uses. Providing a large lateral elevation may create height differences between the street and land uses. In particular, the elevation may hinder access to buildings.

Elevating the roadway may complicate the comfort of boarding and alighting passengers from buses. Excessive elevation of the roadway may pose a visual nuisance in the urban street. Adjusting the heights and slopes of the sidewalks to the heights and slopes of the road may create a visually preferable layout, but it may complicate pedestrian movement due to crossings.

The elevation of the sidewalk may pose a visual hazard in the urban street. Adjusting the visual aspect of the heights and slopes of the sidewalks to the heights and slopes of the road may create a visually preferable layout, but it may complicate pedestrian movement due to the transitions in the slopes on the sidewalks. Principles for implementing elevations in streets and roads with adjacent buildings, except in cases where the maximum elevation in urban streets and roads with adjacent buildings is 5% as specified below.
In urban streets that pass through built-up areas and are bounded by curbs on both sides in such a way that providing elevation may complicate road drainage, or when the lateral elevation may hinder bus or pedestrian activity, it is possible to maintain the standard cross-section suitable for the straight section in the horizontal curve. In this case, the radius of the curve will be larger, as detailed in section 4.3.2 below.
In urban roads and collector streets that pass through open areas.

In areas with pedestrian traffic, the standard cross-section suitable for a straight section can be maintained in the horizontal curve. In this case, the radius of the curve will be larger, as detailed in section 4.3.2 below. On urban roads and collector streets that pass through open areas where drainage is surface-level on the sides of the road, and where a uniform speed can be developed due to a lack of intersections, the pavement should be elevated with circular arches, see also section 4.3.1.3. In road sections where, due to a combination of a large longitudinal slope and significant lateral elevation, there is a need for special upper treatment before the pavement with a weighted slope of 8% or more, measures should be taken to prevent slipping. 

In any case, the elevation policy along that street should be uniform; therefore, if no elevation is provided in a specific section along the street, no elevation will be provided in other sections along that street either. 

Consideration should be given to pedestrian traffic - large elevations should not be implemented across sidewalks and across sections that have crosswalks and crossing points. 

Principles for implementing elevations on roads without adjacent construction: 
Even in urban areas, there may occasionally be roads that pass through undeveloped areas, where at least one side of the road will always border a "green" area - public parks, nature reserves, forests, or areas with building restrictions due to infrastructure.

On Unbuilt Adjacent Roads  
Even in urban areas, there may occasionally be roads that pass through unbuilt areas, where at least one side of the road will always border a "green" area - public parks, nature reserves, forests, or areas with building restrictions due to infrastructure, and so on. As a result, it is possible that on at least one side of the road there is no sidewalk at all, or there are paths separated from the road, no intersections or access points for side uses, no planned parking, and no public transportation stations. Therefore, free-flowing traffic at relatively high speeds is expected on such roads. This scenario is typical mainly in hilly or mountainous areas, where there may be a combination with significant slopes along the route, and thus it is advisable to increase the elevations for safety considerations, which also allows for a reduction in the minimum radii to improve the adaptation to the terrain. The maximum possible elevation under these conditions is a minimum radius of the horizontal curve.

Widening at Horizontal Curves
Purpose of the Widening
Widening of the roadway at horizontal curves is necessary to allow vehicles to travel through the curve under conditions similar to traveling on a straight section of road. The required width for the roadway is composed of the following factors:
A. Width of the design vehicle.
B. The safety margin required to separate two vehicles traveling towards each other.
C. The safety margin between vehicles and the sidewalk or the edges of the roadway.
The width required at a horizontal curve is greater than the width required on a straight section, for the following reasons:
A. The turning radius of a vehicle traveling on a circular arc is greater than the turning radius on a straight section (2.2-2.10 Turning radius is the mark left by the wheel in its path - diagrams).
B. When traveling through a curve, the driver finds it difficult to maneuver the vehicle to travel in the center of the lane. The turning radius of the vehicle in a curve depends on the type of vehicle and the radius of the curve; the longer the vehicle, the greater the turning radius, or the greater the distance between its axles, or the longer the front overhang, and the smaller the radius, the greater the need for widening.
It must be ensured that the required widening is reflected in the statutory plans.

In 1987, the Strategic Highway Research Program began the largest and most 
comprehensive pavement performance test in history—the Long-Term Pavement
Performance (LTPP) program.  During the program’s 20-year life, highway agencies
in the United States and 15 other countries will have collected data on pavement
condition, climate, and traffic volumes and loads from more than 1,000 pavement
test sections.  That information will allow pavement engineers to design better,
longer-lasting roads.
This manual was developed to provide a consistent, uniform basis for collecting
distress data for the LTPP program.

This manual provides a common language for describing cracks, potholes, rutting,
spalling, and other pavement distresses being monitored by the LTPP program. 
The manual is divided into three sections, each focusing on a particular type of
pavement: (1) asphalt concrete-surfaced, (2) jointed portland cement concrete, and
(3) continuously reinforced portland cement concrete.  Each distress is clearly
labeled, described, and illustrated.

As a pavement distress dictionary, the manual will improve communications within
the pavement community by fostering more uniform and consistent definitions of

ANCE TO OTHER USERS
As a pavement distress dictionary, the manual will improve communications within
the pavement community by fostering more uniform and consistent definitions of
pavement distress. Highway agencies, airports, parking facilities, and others with
significant investment in pavements will benefit from adopting a standard distress
language.
Colleges and universities will use the manual in highway engineering courses. It
also serves as a valuable training tool for highway agencies. Now when a distress is
labeled “high severity fatigue cracking,” for example, it is clear exactly what is
meant.  Repairs can be planned and executed more efficiently, saving the highway
agency crew time and money.
Although not specifically designed as a pavement management tool, the Distress
Identification Manual can play an important role in a State’s pavement management
program by ridding reports of inconsistencies and variations caused by a lack of
standardized terminology. Most pavement mana

ication Manual can play an important role in a State’s pavement management
program by ridding reports of inconsistencies and variations caused by a lack of
standardized terminology. Most pavement management programs do not need to
collect data at the level of detail and precision required for the LTPP program, nor
are the severity levels used in the manual necessarily appropriate for all pavement
management situations. Thus, you may choose to modify the procedures (but not
the definitions) contained in the manual to meet your specific needs, taking into
account the desired level of detail, accuracy and timeliness of information, available
resources, and predominant types of distress within the study area.

Description
Occurs in areas subjected to repeated traffic loadings (wheel paths).  Can be a
series of interconnected cracks in early stages of development. Develops into
many-sided, sharp-angled pieces, usually less than 0.3 meters (m) on the longest
side, characteristically with a chicken wire/alligator pattern, in later stages.
Must have a quantifiable area.
Severity Levels

An area of crac

ces, usually less than 0.3 meters (m) on the longest
side, characteristically with a chicken wire/alligator pattern, in later stages.

LOW
An area of cracks with no or only a few connecting cracks; cracks are not
spalled or sealed; pumping is not evident.
MODERATE
An area of interconnected cracks forming a complete pattern; cracks may be
slightly spalled; cracks may be sealed; pumping is not evident.
HIGH
An area of moderately or severely spalled interconnected cracks forming a
complete pattern; pieces may move when subjected to traffic; cracks may be
sealed; pumping may be evident.

severity levels existing within an area cannot be distinguished, rate the entire

INTRODUCTION
This appendix provides instructions, data sheets, and distress maps for use 
in visual surveys for the collection of distress information for ACP, JCP, and
CRCP surfaces. Visual distress survey procedures have been used in the LTPP
program as the primary distress data collection method since 1995. The Distress
Identification Manual for the Long-Term Pavemen

P surfaces. Visual distress survey procedures have been used in the LTPP
program as the primary distress data collection method since 1995. The Distress
Identification Manual for the Long-Term Pavement Performance Program is the
basis for all distress surveys performed for the LTPP.
During the visual distress survey, safety is the first consideration, as with all
field data collection activities. All raters must adhere to the practices and
authority of the State or Canadian Province.
EQUIPMENT FOR DISTRESS SURVEYS
The following equipment is necessary for performing field distress surveys of
any pavement surface type.
• Copy of map sheets and survey forms from most recent prior survey.
• Pavement thermometer.
• Extra blank data sheets and maps.
• Pencils.
• Latest version of the Distress Identification Manual.
• Clipboard.
• Two tape measures, one at least 30 m long and a scale or ruler graduated in
millimeters.
• Calculator.
• Hard hat or safety cap and safety vest.
• Faultmeter, calib

entification Manual.
• Clipboard.
• Two tape measures, one at least 30 m long and a scale or ruler graduated in
millimeters.
• Calculator.
• Hard hat or safety cap and safety vest.
• Faultmeter, calibration stand and manual for PCC test sections.
• Digital camera, video camera, tapes.
• Transverse profile equipment required for AC test sections.
• Longitudinal profile equipment is required on sites where the LTPP
Profilometer is unable to test.
INSTRUCTIONS FOR COMPLETING DISTRESS MAPS
The distress maps show the exact location of each distress type existing on the
test section. The distress types and severity levels should be identified by using
the Distress Identification Manual. A total of five sheets are used to map; each
sheet contains two 15.25-m maps which represent 30.5 m of the test section
(with the exception of SPS-6 sections 2 and 5, which are 305 m).
Each test section must be laid out consistently each time a survey is conducted.
Sections begin and end at the stations marke

t section
(with the exception of SPS-6 sections 2 and 5, which are 305 m).
Each test section must be laid out consistently each time a survey is conducted.
Sections begin and end at the stations marked on the pavement. Lateral extent
of the section, for survey purposes, will vary depending on the existence of
longitudinal joints and cracks and the relative position of the lane markings.
Figures A1 and A2 illustrate the rules to follow when determining the lateral
extent of the section for a distress survey. The lateral extent of the test sections
should be consistent with prior distress surveys. On widened PCC sections, the
lateral extent of the test section includes the full width (4.3 m) of the slab
measured from the centerline longitudinal joint to the shoulder joint. The
lateral extent of AC test sections with double yellow lines on the centerline are
determined by using the inside yellow line.

To map the test section, place the tape measure on the shoulder adjacent to the

INTRODUCTION
Measurement of Faulting in the LTPP Program
This manual is intended for use by the FHWA-LTPP Regional Coordination
Office personnel and others responsible for using the faultmeter to measure
JCP faulting, and for measuring lane-to-shoulder dropoff on LTPP pavement
test sites.
The change in joint faulting and lane-to-shoulder dropoff with time are important
indicators of pavement performance. The digital faultmeters will be used to
collect this data. It is the responsibility of each regional coordination office
contractor to store, maintain, and operate their faultmeter for fault

formance. The digital faultmeters will be used to
collect this data. It is the responsibility of each regional coordination office
contractor to store, maintain, and operate their faultmeter for faulting and
lane-to-shoulder dropoff data collection.
The Georgia Digital Faultmeter
The electronic digital faultmeter was designed to simplify measuring concrete
joint faulting. This meter was designed, developed and built by the Georgia
Department of Transportation Office of Materials and Research personnel 1. The
faultmeter is very light and easy to use. The unit, shown in figure 1, weighs
approximately 3.2 kg and supplies a digital readout with the push of a button
located on the carrying handle. It reads out directly in millimeters (e.g., a
digital readout of “6” indicates 6 mm of faulting) and shows whether the reading
is positive or negative. The unit reads out in 1 second and freezes the r eading
in display so that it can be removed from the road before reading for safer
operation. The

nd shows whether the reading
is positive or negative. The unit reads out in 1 second and freezes the r eading
in display so that it can be removed from the road before reading for safer
operation. The legs of the faultmeter’s base are set on the slab in the direction
of traffic on the “leave side” of the joint. The measuring probe contacts the slab
on the approach. Movement of this probe is transmitted to a Linear Variance
Displacement Transducer to measure joint faulting. The joint must be centered
between the guidelines shown on the side of the meter.
Any slab that is lower on the leave side of the joint will register as a positive
faulting number. If the slab leaving the joint is higher, the meter gives a
negative reading.
The amount of time it takes to complete the faulting survey of a LTPP test sec-
tion depends on the number of joints and cracks encountered, and on the
amount of time needed to measure and record the location of each joint and
crack. Generally, it should take less

LTPP test sec-
tion depends on the number of joints and cracks encountered, and on the
amount of time needed to measure and record the location of each joint and
crack. Generally, it should take less than 30 minutes to measure and record
faulting and lane-to-shoulder dropoff on a 150-m test section using this device.
The Mechanical Faultmeter
The mechanical faultmeter was designed as a backup to the Georgia Faultmeter. It
is not intended for use as a primary measuring device for faulting. The mechanical
faultmeter has the same “footprint” as the Georgia Faultmeter and should be used
in a similar manner. It has a dial indicator instead of the Georgia Faultmeter’s
electronic digital readout. The mechanical faultmeter also does not take
negative faulting readings, and must be reversed to read negative faulting.

centered approximately between the two marks on each side of the meter.

C.1 INTRODUCTION
The Face Company Dipstick is a manually operated device that collects
precision profile measurements at rates greater than traditional rod and level
survey procedures. However, the profile obtained from Dipstick measurements
may have a shift from the true profile because of systematic cumulative errors
in the Dipstick readings. The body of the Dipstick houses an inclinometer
(pendulum), liquid crystal display panels, and a battery for power supply. The
Dipstick sensor is mounted in such a way that its axis and line passing through
footpad contact points are coplanar. The sensor becomes unbalanced as the
Dipstick is pivoted from one leg to the other as it is moved down the pavement,
causing the disp

axis and line passing through
footpad contact points are coplanar. The sensor becomes unbalanced as the
Dipstick is pivoted from one leg to the other as it is moved down the pavement,
causing the display to become blank. After the sensor achieves equilibrium, the
difference in elevation between the two points is displayed. Swivel footpads
with a diameter of 32 mm should be used for all measurements. 
Each LTPP Regional Support Contractor (RSC) has two Dipsticks; a manual
Dipstick (Model 1500) and an automated Dipstick (Model 2000). Both these
Dipsticks display data in millimeters. The spacing between the two feet of the
Dipstick is 305 mm for both models. When the automated Dipstick is used for
data collection, it should be used in manual mode, with data recorded
manually.
Profile measurements on General Pavement Studies (GPS) and SPS sites that
cannot be obtained using the LTPP profiler should be completed using the
Dipstick. Decisions with respect to the need for Dipstick measurement

ents on General Pavement Studies (GPS) and SPS sites that
cannot be obtained using the LTPP profiler should be completed using the
Dipstick. Decisions with respect to the need for Dipstick measurements at
these test sections should be made on a case-by-case basis by responsible
RSC personnel.

single person can collect the data if that person uses a voice activated tape
recorder to record the readings.

C.3.5.5 Closure Error Computation
The total accumulated error in a transverse profile is established by a closed-
loop survey. The forward and return runs along a transverse line are used to
compute this error. At each station, add the readings for the forward and return
runs separately, and record the values in the “Sum” column of form DS-8. Then
at each station, add the values in “Sum” column for the forward and return run,
and record the result in the “Closure” column. At each station, for each
Dipstick reading, add the reading for the forward and return runs, and record
the value in the field “Difference.”

forward and return runs) by 0.076 (0.076 mm is the allowabl

Introduction  
An emergency situation is an external condition that poses a threat to human life or the lives of relatives and disrupts the functional, cognitive, and emotional continuity of the individual, family, group, and community.  
A municipal call center, by its nature, deals with a reality of "emergency routine" – a work routine in which behind every call there may be an emergency situation. Therefore, it must be prepared to deal, at any time, with two types of emergency situations:  
1. Emergency situations/exceptional events during routine – such as a major water main break that disrupts water supply to many streets for long hours; a fire in a business that contains hazardous materials.

and also deal, at all times, with two types of emergency situations:
1. Emergency situations/exceptional events during routine – such as a large water main break that disrupts water supply to many streets for long hours; a fire in a business that contains hazardous materials; a traffic accident that blocks a major traffic route, etc.
2. Emergency situations during an emergency – natural disaster, state of war, earthquake, and mass casualty events.
The main difference between the two types of emergencies is that in a routine emergency, a specific emergency situation is identified for a resident or a group of residents. In summary, the responsibility of the municipal center manager is to create managerial and functional capabilities in the municipal center that allow for as smooth a transition as possible from a routine situation to a variety of emergency situations and optimal and professional functioning of all role holders operating within it over time. To this end, they must be familiar with the municipal and national emergency procedures, understand their implications for the functioning of the municipal center during emergencies and their personal functioning, and proactively act to meet all the derived implications.

The success of the municipal center in fulfilling its role during emergencies is the result of meticulous preparations and ongoing and regular training of the municipal center employees and their drills.

The work method for a report regarding the removal of a carcass:
1. The dispatcher will ensure that the carcass is located in a public area, will receive its exact location, and will inform the resident how long the removal will take.
2. The dispatcher will enter the report into the computer system under the Environmental Services Department, subject of carcass removal.
3. The dispatcher will call the carcass removal duty officer and update him on the details of the report.
4. The duty officer will remove the carcass within the defined timeframe. If he does not find the carcass, he must make direct contact with the resident and update him on the results of his inspection.

Pavement Condition Index (PCI)
PCI is a numerical rating of the pavement condition based on the type and severity of distresses
observed on the pavement surface. The PCI value of the pavement condition is represented by a
numerical index between 0 and 100, where 0 is the worst possible condition and 100 is the best
possible condition.
PCI is calculated based on the distresses observed during condition surveys (inspections). This
information is used to determine the proper deduct values and to calculate the PCI values of a
pavement section. 
The PCI history of a pavement section can help establish its rate of deterioration and identify future
major rehabilitation needs. PCI values are also used in prioritizing, funding and executing Maintenance
and Rehabilitation (M&R) on the pavement section.

The company's maintenance work consists of several stages, as detailed below:  
Routine maintenance: The goals of routine maintenance are to preserve the road and its systems at a good and stable service level over time; to maintain and improve travel safety; to preserve and enhance the road's appearance. Routine maintenance activities include cleaning roads and infrastructure, installing and maintaining safety barriers, gardening and pruning, road marking, signage, drainage system repairs, preventing slipperiness of pavements, pothole treatment, and more.  
Preventive maintenance: Preventive maintenance involves planning and executing work to prevent deterioration in the functionality of roads and road structures, thereby reducing the risk of failure phenomena in the future. The planning of preventive maintenance is based on data from the company's computerized systems. Preventive maintenance activities include, among other things, road resurfacing, performing repairs on pavements, and rehabilitating road structures.  
Breakdown maintenance: Breakdown maintenance is carried out at points where it is found that transportation use may cause damage to property and even risk human life.

Maintenance of Pavements and Road Surfacing  
As noted in the company's documents, performing maintenance actions on time contributes to slowing the deterioration rate of the pavement - the upper part of the road - thereby extending its lifespan. Furthermore, carrying out these actions at the right time also helps maintain a high level of service for the road over time and saves significantly on maintenance costs, which increase as the condition of the pavement deteriorates over the years. A paved road is subject to physical pressures from traffic loads and the effects of weather. The structure of the pavement, its cost, and its lifespan depend on the thickness and quality of the processed layers, the desired level of service (quality and comfort of travel under safety conditions), maintenance measures during the service period, traffic load forecasts during this period, and environmental conditions, including the type of soil on which the pavement is built. According to the recommendation of an international expert hired by the company, and in accordance with global standards, pavements should be maintained "once every 8 to 10 years, meaning at least 10% of the network [of roads] each year" (emphasis in the original). Bridge Maintenance  
A bridge is an engineering structure supported by piers and located above a physical obstacle or depression, such as a stream, road, or railway, serving as a passage for carrying mobile loads like vehicles, trains, and pedestrians. Maintaining the engineering condition and proper functionality of bridges and adhering to the standards for which they were designed will help prevent defects and ensure the safety of their users. Additionally, the collapse of a bridge poses a danger to passersby and significant economic costs. Damage caused to a bridge due to neglect may be irreversible or its repair may not be economically viable. To avoid this, proactive measures must be taken, such as regular engineering inspections, monitoring work, and maintenance work on the bridge.  
This is reflected in a periodic report by the National Roads Company for the year 2019: "The company maintains over 6,500 road structures of various types (vehicle and pedestrian bridges, signage bridges, culverts, and walls), including about 600 vehicle bridges and approximately 78 pedestrian bridges. Each year, the company conducts various surveys regarding the engineering condition of the inventory under its responsibility. These surveys are carried out periodically, using advanced technologies including sophisticated equipment for detecting and interpreting damages on the road, structural strength tests, and measurements of flatness and slopes in the pavement. Additionally, inspections are conducted...

"Inventory management of the bridges under its responsibility. These surveys are conducted periodically, using advanced technologies including sophisticated equipment for identifying and interpreting road damage, structural strength tests, and assessing the smoothness and slopes of the pavement. Additionally, visual engineering reviews are conducted for bridges and road structures at the component and sub-component level of the structure.

To maintain the bridges under its responsibility, the company has developed guidelines for bridge inspections and is engaged in developing a management system for their maintenance. The company has a bridge management unit that is responsible, among other things, for ongoing monitoring of the engineering condition of the bridges. This monitoring is carried out through regular and scheduled inspections, which allow for the examination of the physical and functional condition of the bridge components. If defects are found in the components, the unit must assess their severity, determine what actions need to be taken for the maintenance of the bridge, indicate the urgency of these actions, and alert to hazardous situations that require immediate attention. Through ongoing monitoring of the bridge inventory, it is possible to plan maintenance and rehabilitation actions and establish a priority scale for their execution. Planning maintenance actions will allow for the correction of deficiencies in components before they lead to failure and prevent a situation where the damage to a component or even to the entire bridge is so severe that repairing the bridge would not be economically viable."

Maintenance of Lighting Equipment  
Driving at night affects orientation, reaction time, and the performance of the driver. In such driving conditions, the quality of lighting and the quality of the road surface are of great importance. For nighttime driving to be safe, infrastructure must allow the driver to see further than what the vehicle's headlights provide. At intersections on intercity roads, where merging onto the road is already difficult, lighting is particularly important. According to publications from the Ministry of Transportation, good lighting can lead to an average reduction of about 30% in traffic accidents during nighttime hours. According to the Ministry of Transportation's guidelines from 1996, there is an obligation to install lighting at the following locations: every intersection, even near sections of road that are not illuminated along their length; continuous road sections between intersections where the distance between them does not exceed one kilometer; transition lighting at the approaches to the intersection; any location of security or safety significance.

Road Markings
Roadside signage is included in the traffic management system of the road network and is part of the valid signage board. Road signs are intended to convey various messages to road users, and they are important to ensure the safe flow of traffic. The meaning of the markings pertains to all road users, including drivers and pedestrians. The functional and safety importance of markings on the road is particularly evident at night and in adverse weather conditions. An insufficient level of visibility of the markings may lead road users to make incorrect decisions while driving, decisions that increase the risk of accidents. An example of this is the inadequate marking of crosswalks. 
The previous audit report found that the marking materials used by the National Roads Company are of the "simple" type - single-component paint. These materials are characterized by a short lifespan (6 - 12 months) and an insufficient level of slip resistance (friction coefficient). These characteristics force the company to perform increased maintenance: repainting at intersections every six months, standard painting on roads once a year, and on busy roads - even more frequently. These actions are accompanied by road closures that disrupt regular traffic, and these disruptions create economic damages in addition to the inconvenience.

Marking at intersections is done once every six months, standard painting on roads once a year, and on busy roads - even more frequently. The processes for monitoring the marking in the field are based on visual inspection (day and night visibility). 

The previous audit report noted that in November 2014, the Transportation Planning Division of the Ministry of Transportation published guidelines for the selection and application of standard materials for road marking, aimed at upgrading the marking method on the road network in Israel - in terms of standards, material quality, durability, and safety characteristics derived from this, as well as to ensure that the performance values of the marking materials meet the requirements. Additionally, according to these guidelines, the company is required to use two-component marking materials with a long lifespan, or permanent sheets whose durability is estimated at 3 - 5 years. 

Additional advantages of the two-component marking materials specified in the new guidelines are more effective resistance to vehicle skidding and greater light reflection over longer distances during nighttime driving. According to the new guidelines, the company was required to prepare for the implementation of the new standards by 31.12.14.

Summary  
The maintenance of roads, bridges, and infrastructure is of great importance in many aspects: road safety, preventing the depreciation of the economic value of roads, and preventing greater future damage to them, benefits from saving travel time for road users, and more. Road maintenance is particularly important due to the increase in traffic and the high congestion on the country's roads, as well as the significant investment made in recent decades that has increased the length of roads and the number of bridges that need maintenance. To carry out maintenance activities, the Israel National Roads Company requires a dedicated budget that will allow it to optimally maintain transportation infrastructure.  
The follow-up audit revealed that the company acted to correct deficiencies identified in the previous audit report. Most of the deficiencies that were not corrected stemmed from a reduction in the maintenance budget.  
As noted in the previous audit report, the Ministry of Transportation and the Ministry of Finance, in collaboration with the company, should examine whether the allocation of funds for road maintenance adequately meets the needs, especially in light of the new maintenance model developed by the company in 2017. They should also check whether the distribution of the budget among the areas is carried out optimally. These actions are essential to enable the company to improve areas where there is still a gap between the desired and the actual, particularly in the areas of road maintenance, resurfacing, road markings, and road lighting.

Road Maintenance by Local Authorities  
Introduction  
The laws governing local authorities establish the obligation and authority of the local authority to develop, pave, and maintain the public roads within its jurisdiction. The road infrastructure within the jurisdiction of a local authority includes roads with different functional characteristics: (a) main roads - roads that facilitate traffic to and from the local authority and between different areas of the authority, with a high traffic load compared to other roads; (b) secondary roads - roads that facilitate traffic from neighborhoods within the authority to the main roads, with a medium traffic load compared to other roads; (c) access roads - roads within neighborhoods that connect to collector roads (secondary), with a low traffic load compared to other roads.  
A paved road is subject to physical pressures due to traffic loads and is affected by weather conditions. The upper part of the road that bears the pressures and loads - the wearing course - consists of processed layers of subbase, base, and asphalt (a lower layer and an upper layer) laid on the subgrade.

Physical stresses due to traffic loads and influenced by weather conditions. The upper part of the road bearing the stresses and loads - the pavement - consists of processed layers of subbase, base, and asphalt (lower layer and upper layer) laid on the subgrade. There may be different pavement structures, each with different costs and life expectancies. The structure of the pavement, its cost, and its service period depend on the thickness of the processed layers and their quality, the desired level of service (the quality and comfort of the ride under safety conditions), maintenance measures during the service period, traffic load forecasts during this period, and environmental conditions, including the type of soil on which the pavement is built. According to the 2021 report of the ITF - International Transport Forum at the OECD - road infrastructure maintenance has gained increased importance in recent years, and many governments are interested in establishing road maintenance policies that can provide better returns on investment. Various infrastructures are beginning to be interconnected, and the demand for them is increasing as more and more people use them. This fact accelerates the aging and wear of the infrastructures, which increases the need for maintenance actions. The impacts of climate change exacerbate the condition of road infrastructures.

Normative background  
Section 249 of the Municipalities Ordinance [New Version] (hereinafter - the Municipalities Ordinance) establishes the authority of the municipality to pave any street that is not private property, ensure its proper condition, and pave sidewalks. According to Section 235 of the Municipalities Ordinance, it is the municipality's duty to supervise the construction of every street and ensure its repair and maintenance, to prevent obstacles in the streets and remove them, as well as to take appropriate safety measures against accidents during the construction or repair of streets, pits, or channels.  
The authority of a local council and a regional council to pave and maintain public roads within their jurisdiction derives from their general powers to act on any matter concerning the public within their jurisdiction, including the development and improvement of the council's jurisdiction.  
In Section 1 of the Traffic Ordinance [New Version], "road" is defined as: "including any track, way, street, alley, square, passage, bridge, or open place that the public has the right to pass through." In Section 1 of the Traffic Regulations, 1961, "urban road" is defined as: "any road within the area located in the jurisdiction of a local authority or local authorities bordering each other, and at the entrance to that area, a sign is placed indicating 'entrance to the area of an urban road,' and up to the place where..."

In the 1961 law, "urban road" is defined as follows: "Any road within an area that falls under the jurisdiction of a local authority or local authorities that border each other, and at the entrance to that area, a sign is placed indicating 'Entering the urban road area', and up to the point where a sign is placed indicating 'End of urban road area'." 

In the jurisprudence, it has been determined that the local authority is responsible for maintaining public roads within its jurisdiction in a proper condition, and it has a duty of care towards users of those roads. It has also been established in the jurisprudence that the local authority must take reasonable precautions to prevent harm to users of public roads - ensuring the proper condition of the roads serving the general public, developing the roads, and maintaining them.

Methods for Road Maintenance
The manner of road maintenance should be determined based on indicators that reflect the quality of the roads and the level of service required from them. These indicators reflect the amount of damage caused to the roads over the years, the type of damage, and the severity of that damage. 

The Pavement Condition Index (PCI) is an index that quantitatively defines the condition of the pavement based on the type of damage caused to it, its quantity, and severity, with values ranging from 0 to 100 (0 - in a ruined condition, 100 - in excellent condition). The index is based on

Pavement Condition Index (hereinafter - PCI) is an index that quantitatively defines the condition of the pavement based on the type of damage caused to it, its quantity, and severity, with values ranging from 0 to 100 (0 - destroyed condition, 100 - excellent condition). The index is based on conducting a visual damage survey of asphalt and rigid concrete pavements ("Paver Method Damage Survey"). The damage survey is carried out using a dedicated collection vehicle equipped with downward-facing video cameras for the purpose of photographing the damages.
